1.title: Digital data
terms: Raw facts and figures that have no meaning or context on their own.
Data that has been processed and given context so that it has meaning.
Hardware and software working together to take data as input, process it and produce information as output.
A number system with only two digits, 0 and 1, used by computers because their switches are either off or on.
A binary digit: the smallest unit of digital data, either a 0 or a 1.
A group of 8 bits; one character such as a letter, digit or punctuation mark is stored in one byte.
A group of 4 bits (half a byte); it can store one hexadecimal digit.
The amount of data a storage device or memory can hold, measured in bytes and multiples such as GB and TB.
American Standard Code for Information Interchange: a character set that gives each letter, digit and punctuation mark a unique binary code.
A single letter, digit, punctuation mark or symbol. As a data type, exactly one such symbol, stored using its code from the character set.
An agreed list of characters in which each character has its own unique binary code.
A large character set that can represent characters from most of the world's writing systems, as well as symbols and emoji.
The kind of data a field can hold, e.g. Short Text, Number, Currency or Date/Time; it controls what can be entered and what can be done with the data.
A data type that stores dates and/or times so they can be sorted, calculated with and displayed in different formats.
A data type for whole numbers, positive or negative, with no decimal or fractional part.
A data type for numbers that can have a decimal or fractional part, positive or negative; real numbers also include whole numbers.
A data type for a sequence of characters (letters, digits and symbols) of variable length.
A validation check that makes sure data is of the correct data type, e.g. numeric, text or date.
A data type that can hold only one of two values, such as Yes/No or True/False.
A database data type for money values, displayed with a currency symbol and two decimal places.
An image stored as a grid of pixels, with the colour code of every pixel plus metadata such as width and height; it pixelates when enlarged.
The number of bits used to store the colour of each pixel; n bits give 2ⁿ possible colours.
Data about data, e.g. the width, height and colour depth of an image, stored so the file can be rebuilt correctly.
Short for picture element: the smallest element of a digital image that can be displayed or edited; each pixel holds one colour stored as a binary code.
Reducing the size of a file so it needs less storage and can be uploaded or downloaded more quickly.
The blocky appearance of a bitmap image when it is enlarged too much, because the individual pixels become visible.
Pixels per inch (screens) and dots per inch (printing): units used to measure resolution.
The number of pixels in an image, given as width × height or as pixels per inch; more pixels give a sharper image but a larger file.
An image stored as a list of objects (lines, curves and shapes) with properties such as position, size, line colour and fill colour; it can be resized without losing quality.
A signal that varies smoothly and continuously, representing a physical quantity such as a sound wave.
A device that converts an analogue signal, such as sound from a microphone, into digital (binary) data by sampling it at regular intervals.
The number of bits used to store each sound sample; more bits give more possible levels, so each sample is recorded more accurately.
The number of samples of a sound taken each second, measured in hertz (Hz); CD audio uses 44 100 Hz.
Measuring the level of an analogue signal at regular time intervals; each reading is rounded and stored as a binary number.
The number of bits of data processed for each second of sound, usually in kilobits per second; equals sample rate × bit depth for each channel.
Sound recorded on two channels (left and right); it needs twice the data of the same sound in mono (one channel).
An area of memory that temporarily stores the next part of a video or song before it is played, so playback continues if the connection slows or drops briefly.
Playing video or audio over the internet while it is still being received, without first downloading and permanently storing the whole file.
Comma-separated values: a text format in which each line is a record and fields are separated by commas; used to move table data between spreadsheets and databases.
The ability to move data between computers or software applications without having to re-enter it, usually by saving it in a standard file format.
The standard way data is organised inside a file, shown by its file extension (e.g. .jpg, .csv), which decides which programs can open it.
An image format using lossy compression whose level the user can choose; gives small files and is widely used for photographs on web pages.
Musical Instrument Digital Interface: stores and exchanges musical instructions (notes, instruments, timing) between electronic instruments and computers, not recorded sound.
Portable Document Format, developed by Adobe: keeps a document's fonts, images and layout the same on any device; usually read-only.
Rich Text Format: a document format with basic formatting that can be opened by different word processors and operating systems.
Tagged Image File Format: stores high-quality bitmap images that can move between Windows and Apple computers; files are larger than JPEGs.
A standard uncompressed audio format; high quality but large files.
Compression that reduces file size without losing any data, so the file can be restored exactly to the original, e.g. ZIP, PNG.
Compression that reduces file size by permanently removing some data, so quality is reduced and the original cannot be fully restored, e.g. JPEG, MP3.
tips: In a 'describe the difference' question, define both terms and give an example of each. Your information example must include the context in words, not just more numbers.
Learn the order by heart: bit, nibble, byte, KB, MB, GB, TB. Ordering and matching questions on these units come up regularly for quick marks.
Show every line of working and write the unit with each number. Method marks are given even if a slip spoils the final answer.
For 'Why does a computer use ASCII codes?' give two points: computers only understand binary, so each character needs a unique code; and a shared standard lets text move between devices correctly.
For 'describe a data type', say what it stores and give an example, e.g. 'Real stores numbers with a decimal part, such as a price of 3.49.'
An 'explain' question needs a reason and a consequence: 'so that calculations can be carried out on numeric fields, such as totalling sales'.
In database questions, software names such as Short Text, Number, Currency, Date/Time and Yes/No are also credited, but stick to the specification names unless the question uses database terms.
Define a pixel as 'the smallest element of a digital image that can be displayed or edited'. Calling it 'a dot' alone is too vague for the mark.
In an 'explain' question, link resolution to both quality and file size: 'more pixels means more detail, but each pixel must be stored, so the file is larger'.
When describing how a vector is stored, say 'objects and their properties' and name at least two properties, such as position and fill colour.
For 'describe two differences', each mark needs both sides: 'a bitmap is made of pixels, whereas a vector is made of objects and their properties'. One-sided statements usually score nothing.
Write the formula first, substitute the numbers, then convert one step at a time with units. Method marks are available at each step.
To 'define the purpose of an ADC', say it converts an analogue signal into digital (binary) data so the computer can process it, and mention that it does this by sampling at regular intervals.
For each factor give a definition, then say what increasing it does to quality and file size. Answers that mention only quality usually miss a mark.
Write the formula, substitute, then convert one step at a time with units. If you get a tiny number like 0.0003 MB or a huge one like 30 000 MB for a short clip, check your working.
Marks for buffering come from three ideas: the buffer is temporary memory; it stores the next part of the video in advance; and playback continues from it if the connection slows or drops.
A strong answer defines portability and links it to a standard file format with an example, e.g. exporting a database table as csv to open in a spreadsheet.
'Justify' means give a feature of the format that fits the task. 'JPEG because it is good' scores nothing; 'JPEG because its compression gives small files that load quickly on a web page' scores.

For 'Explain how compression can assist in uploading a file', link the smaller file to a benefit: less data to send, so it uploads faster and uses less bandwidth; it may also get under an upload size limit.
When comparing, always state that lossy loses data permanently whereas lossless can be restored exactly, then give an example of each.

2.title: Software
terms: Software designed to let the user carry out a specific task, such as word processing, editing photos or browsing the web.
Off-the-shelf software made for many users with common needs; low cost, ready to use straight away and widely supported, e.g. Microsoft Word.
Software that runs and manages the computer hardware and provides a platform for application programs, e.g. the operating system, utilities and device drivers.
Bespoke software written for one organisation's specific needs; fits exactly but is expensive and slow to develop because one customer pays for all of it.
System software that manages the computer's resources – allocating memory, storage and processing time – so that the hardware and application software can work together.
A short, fixed period of processor time given to a task or user before the processor moves on to the next one.
The steps when a computer is switched on: start-up instructions in ROM run, the hardware is tested, and the operating system is found on storage and loaded into RAM.
Similar data is collected into batches over a period of time and processed together later, without human involvement, often overnight, e.g. bills or payroll.
A permanent or semi-permanent file of main records, such as customer details and previous readings, that is updated from a transaction file during batch processing.
Each input is processed as soon as it is entered and files are updated at once, so the output is produced in time to affect the next input, e.g. ticket booking.
A temporary file holding the data collected for a batch, such as meter readings with account numbers, used to update the master file.
A system in which many users at different terminals share the processor of one powerful computer, each being given a time slice in turn.
A scheduling method in which each task or user is given a time slice of the processor in a fixed order, returning to the first after the last.
Copying data back from a backup to return the data or system to an earlier state.
A utility that divides processor time between tasks (e.g. by round robin) and runs jobs such as backups, scans or updates automatically at set times.
A small system program that carries out one specific task to help the operating system maintain, protect or speed up the computer, e.g. defragmenter, task scheduler, backup, antivirus.
A utility that rearranges the blocks on a disk so each file is stored in adjacent blocks and free space is grouped together, speeding up file access.
When the blocks of a file are stored in separate, non-adjacent places on a disk because there is not enough continuous free space.
A copy of data stored separately from the original, preferably off-site, so it can be restored if the original is lost or damaged.
A backup in which all the data is copied; simple to restore but slow and needs a lot of storage.
A backup that copies only the data changed since the last backup; quick and small, but restoring needs the last full backup plus every incremental since.
Utility software that scans files and incoming data, compares them with a database of known virus signatures, and removes or quarantines threats; it must be updated regularly.
Isolating an infected file so it cannot run or spread, while keeping it in case it turns out to be safe.
A harmful program that attaches itself to a file and, when the file is opened, copies itself to other files and computers, possibly damaging data or performance.
tips: For a 'distinguish' question give one point about each type and an example of each – for example 'System software manages the hardware, e.g. Windows; application software lets the user perform a task, e.g. Excel.'
'Describe' needs more than a list. For each resource, name it and say what the OS does with it – e.g. 'it allocates processing time by giving each task a time slice in turn'.
For three marks, aim for three separate steps in the correct order and use the words ROM, test/check hardware, and load the OS into RAM.
For three marks: many users/terminals share one processor (1), each is given a time slice in turn (1), switching is so fast each user appears to have continuous access (1).

In 6-mark 'discuss' questions, the top band needs the correct mode for each task with a clear, context-linked reason – and a sentence on why the other mode would be unsuitable is a good way to show depth.

A full 'explain' answer has a cause (files split into blocks stored where space is free), an effect (head moves more, slower access) and the fix (blocks moved together, free space grouped, faster access).
When describing a procedure, say how often, when, which type, and where copies are stored – each is a separate creditworthy point.
For 'why update?' give both halves of the argument: new viruses are always being created AND the software can only detect viruses whose signatures it holds.

3.title: Database applications
terms: A primary key made up of two or more fields that together uniquely identify each record.
An organised, structured collection of related data that can be searched, sorted and presented, usually held in one or more tables.
A single item of data stored for every record, forming one column of a table and identified by its field name.
A field whose value is unique for every record, used to identify each record in a table; it must never be blank.
All of the related data about one person or item, forming one row in a table; a record is made up of fields.
A database structure that stores data about one type of thing, organised in rows (records) and columns (fields).
The unnecessary repetition of the same data in a database, wasting storage and risking inconsistent copies.
A database that holds all its data in a single two-dimensional table, which often leads to repeated data.
A database in which data is held in several tables, each about one thing, linked together by relationships.
A field in one table that holds the primary key values of another table, used to link the two tables.
A link between two tables made through a common field – the primary key of one table stored as a foreign key in the other.
A symbol drawn at the 'many' end of a relationship line; Access uses the infinity sign (∞) instead.
A relationship in which one record in a table links to many records in another, but each of those links back to only one, e.g. one customer makes many bookings.
A rule enforced on a relationship that keeps linked tables consistent, e.g. a foreign key value must match an existing primary key, so there are no orphan records.
The conditions a record must meet to be included in a query's results, e.g. DailyRate >= 20.
An on-screen layout used to enter new records, edit existing records or view records in a database.
A small stored program that carries out a repetitive task automatically, usually run by clicking a button.
A database tool that searches tables and extracts the records that meet set criteria.
A database tool that presents data from a table or query in a formatted, user-friendly layout for printing or display, often grouped and sorted.
To bring data into a database from another file, such as a csv file or spreadsheet, instead of retyping it.
A data type that lets files, such as a digital photo, be attached to a record.
A data type, often used for a key field, in which the computer creates a new sequential number automatically for each record.
A data type that stores the result of a calculation using other fields in the same record.
A data type that stores a link to a web address (URL) or an email address.
Creates a drop-down list of values so the user chooses an entry rather than typing it.
Object Linking and Embedding: a data type for an object created in other software, such as a spreadsheet or word-processed document.
A data type that holds one of only two values (a Boolean), such as Yes/No or True/False.
An automatic check made by the computer as data is input, to ensure it is sensible, reasonable and within allowed limits; invalid data is rejected. It cannot confirm data is correct.
The error message shown when data breaks a validation rule, explaining what is allowed.
A check that data has been entered or copied accurately, e.g. by double entry or a visual check against the source.
A validation check that makes sure data matches a set pattern, e.g. a postcode or an email address containing @.
A pattern set on a field that controls which type of character can be typed in each position; used to carry out a format check.
A validation check that makes sure data has an exact number of characters, or is within a minimum and maximum number of characters.
A validation check that makes sure data has been entered, so a field cannot be left blank.
A validation check that makes sure a value lies between a lower and an upper limit.
An expression set on a field that data must satisfy to be accepted, e.g. Between 1 And 8 or Is Not Null.
A logical operator that selects values within a range, including both end values.
A symbol that compares a value with other data, giving true or false: = equal, <> not equal, < less than, <= less than or equal, > greater than, >= greater than or equal.
An operator such as AND, OR or BETWEEN that combines or tests conditions and gives a true or false (Boolean) result.
Data sets so large, fast-arriving and varied that they cannot be stored or analysed by normal database software; described by volume, velocity and variety.
The many different types and formats of data, such as text, images, video and sensor readings, both structured and unstructured.
The speed at which data is created and must be processed, often in real time.
The very large amount of data collected and stored, often terabytes or petabytes.
Data organised in a fixed format, usually fields and records, so it is easy to search and analyse, e.g. dates, names, prices.
Data with no fixed format that cannot easily be processed with normal database tools, e.g. emails, social media posts, photos and videos.
Using algorithms, software or artificial intelligence to examine data and find patterns, trends and relationships so conclusions can be drawn.
Searching very large data sets with software to discover patterns and relationships that were not previously known.
tips: When choosing a key field, name it AND justify it with the word 'unique', and say why an alternative fails – e.g. 'two members could share a surname'.
To explain the difference, describe both structures and then give a consequence – 'so data only needs to be updated in one place'.
A full answer names both tables, the primary key, the foreign key, and describes the link in words – 'one member can make many bookings'.
If asked the purpose of referential integrity, say it keeps data consistent between the tables, then give one specific effect from the scenario.

In 'explain the difference' questions write one sentence for each tool, then a linking sentence, e.g. 'a query could select this month's bookings, and a report would then print them grouped by court'.
For 'what is meant by importing data' give the definition, a source (csv/spreadsheet) and a benefit (saves time, avoids errors).
Start each justification with 'because' and name a property of the data: 'because it contains letters and numbers', 'because it will be used to calculate the total'.
'Range check' alone rarely gets two marks. Write 'a range check so that the number of passengers must be between 1 and 8'.
Test your rule in your head with a value just below, on, and just above each limit before you write it down.
Show your T/F working in the margin. It keeps you accurate and makes the final list quick to check.
A 3-mark question usually gives one mark per V explained. A context-linked example for each makes the meaning unmistakable.
For 'describe the difference', give the defining feature of each and an example of each – four clear points.
For 'explain the need' link back to the three Vs – each V is a reason ordinary methods cannot cope – then give one benefit to the organisation.

4.title: Spreadsheet applications
terms: The box where a column and a row meet; it holds one item of data or one formula.
A block of adjacent cells referred to together, written first cell:last cell, e.g. B5:B12.
The address of a cell, written as its column letter followed by its row number, e.g. H8.
Text entered in a cell to identify what a row or column contains, e.g. Surname or Price.
Application software that organises data in a grid of rows and columns so that it can be calculated, analysed and presented; results recalculate automatically when data changes.
A number entered in a cell so that it can be used in calculations, e.g. 45 or 2.20.
A single spreadsheet file, which can contain one or more worksheets.
One grid of rows and columns inside a workbook, shown on its own tab.
The way a cell's contents are displayed, e.g. General, Number, Currency, Percentage, Date, Time or Text; formatting changes how data looks, not the value stored.
Combining two or more adjacent cells into a single cell and centring the contents across it, e.g. for a title above a table.
Formatting that makes long text continue onto extra lines inside the same cell instead of spilling into the next cell.
A symbol that tells a formula which calculation to do: + add, - subtract, * multiply, / divide, ^ power.
The small square at the bottom right of a selected cell; dragging it replicates the cell's contents or formula into neighbouring cells.

An instruction in a cell to carry out a calculation using operators, values and cell references, e.g. =B2*C2; it always starts with = and the cell shows the result, which updates when referenced cells change.
Copying a formula into neighbouring cells, e.g. by dragging the fill handle or using Fill Down, so the cell references adjust to each new row or column; it saves time and reduces errors.
A function that calculates the arithmetic mean of the numbers in a range, ignoring blank cells, e.g. =AVERAGE(D2:D7).
A function that counts how many cells in a range contain numbers; blank cells and text are not counted.
A function that counts how many cells in a range meet a condition, e.g. =COUNTIF(C2:C40,"Yes").
A built-in, ready-made formula that does a particular job, e.g. SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN, COUNT, COUNTIF, IF or VLOOKUP; the range or values it works on go inside brackets.
A function that returns the highest value in a range, e.g. =MAX(D2:D7).
A function that returns the lowest value in a range, e.g. =MIN(D2:D7).
A function that adds all the numbers in a range, e.g. =SUM(D2:D7).
A cell reference that stays the same when a formula is copied or replicated, shown with $ signs, e.g. $F$1; used for a single fixed value such as a rate.
A cell reference that changes when the formula is replicated, so it points to the matching cell in the new row or column, e.g. B2 becomes B3 when filled down.
Text placed at the top (header) or bottom (footer) of every printed page, e.g. a title, file name, date or page number.
A selected range of cells set as the only part of a worksheet that will be printed.
Formatting (e.g. a fill colour, font colour or icon) that is applied automatically to a cell only when a set condition is met, and changes if the data changes.
A rule applied to cells that checks data as it is entered, so only sensible values within set limits are accepted; it cannot check that the data is correct.
The message shown by data validation when invalid data is entered, asking the user to re-enter valid data.
Bringing data into a spreadsheet from another file or application (e.g. a database table or CSV file), usually with a step-by-step wizard, so it does not have to be retyped.
A pre-designed spreadsheet with its layout, formatting, labels and formulae already set up, used as the starting point for new documents with the same format.
A function that tests a condition and returns one value if it is true and a different value if it is false, e.g. =IF(B2>=40,"Pass","Resit").
An IF function placed inside another IF function so that three or more outcomes are possible.
The range of cells searched by VLOOKUP; the values to be matched must be in its first column.
Vertical lookup: a function that searches for a value in the first column of a table and returns a value from a chosen column in the same row, e.g. =VLOOKUP(B2,$H$2:$J$5,3,FALSE).
A spreadsheet that represents a real situation using input values and formulae that act as rules, so outputs are calculated automatically.
Changing input values (or rules) in a spreadsheet model to see the effect on the outputs and predict what would happen, e.g. changing a price to see the effect on profit.
A visual representation of spreadsheet data, such as a column, line, pie or scatter chart, used to compare values, show trends or show parts of a whole.
The key on a chart that shows which colour or pattern represents each data series.
tips: When a question shows a screenshot, read the column letters and row numbers carefully before writing a range. Count the rows: B5:B12 is eight cells, not seven.

When asked how cells have been formatted, name the feature precisely (e.g. 'merge and centre', 'currency format with two decimal places') and say what it does to those cells. 'Made it look nice' earns nothing.

For 'write the formula for cell X' questions, write the whole thing: =, the correct references and the right operator, e.g. =C5-B5. Check which way round a subtraction should go – 'budget minus spent' is not the same as 'spent minus budget'.
If a question gives values and asks for the result of a function, show the answer in the same format as the data (e.g. £39.60, not 39.6) and double-check with a quick mental sum.

To explain why an absolute reference is used, give both halves: the reference does not change when the formula is replicated, and why that matters here (e.g. every order must use the one discount rate in H1).
For 'describe a feature to improve a printed sheet', name the feature and say what it adds, e.g. 'a footer with page numbers so the pages can be kept in order'.

When describing conditional formatting, give the condition and the format, e.g. 'if stock is below 5, the cell turns red'. For validation, name the check and give the limits, e.g. 'range check: whole number 1–16'.
For 'describe a benefit of a template', explain the benefit in the scenario: 'every coach records fees in the same layout, so the treasurer can combine them easily'.
Write the complete function in the exam: =, IF, brackets, condition, both results in the right order, commas and quotation marks. Each of these can carry a mark.
Examiners have reported weak VLOOKUP explanations. Explain each part in a sentence: what is looked up, where it is searched for, which column is returned, and why FALSE is used.
In a 'how could a model help' answer, describe the steps: enter different values, formulae recalculate the outputs, compare the outcomes, then choose – and link each step to the scenario.
Chart questions often ask for the cell range used. Include the label column, e.g. A2:B7, not just B2:B7, and justify the chart type in one clause.
'Saves time' alone is thin. Explain why: 'the five steps to clear the form are done with one click, so the café can serve the next customer faster'. Macros are also used in databases – see Chapter 3.

5.title: Computer hardware
terms: Central processing unit: a microprocessor whose purpose is to process data and carry out (execute) the instructions of programs, controlling the other parts of the computer.
The repeated process in which the CPU fetches an instruction from main memory, decodes it and then executes it.
A processor whose circuits are all built onto a single chip.
A register in the ALU that holds the result of a calculation before it is stored in memory.
Arithmetic logic unit: the part of the CPU that carries out arithmetic calculations and logical operations and comparisons, e.g. AND, OR, NOT and 'greater than'.
The part of the CPU that fetches and decodes instructions and sends control signals so that they are executed, co-ordinating all the other components.
Main memory that holds the programs and data currently in use; each location has a unique address so the CPU can access it directly.
Instruction address register (CCEA's term): holds the instruction currently being decoded and executed.
Memory address register: holds the address of the memory location being read from or written to.
Memory data register: holds the data or instruction being transferred to or from memory; everything moving between the CPU and memory passes through it.
The register that holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched; it is incremented after each fetch.
A very small, very fast memory location inside the CPU used for one specific purpose.
A small amount of very fast memory inside or next to the CPU that holds frequently used instructions and data, so they need not be fetched from slower RAM.
The number of fetch–execute cycles a CPU can carry out per second, measured in hertz; e.g. 3 GHz = 3 billion cycles per second.
An independent processing unit inside a CPU with its own control unit, ALU and registers, so it can process instructions at the same time as other cores.
A CPU containing two or more cores (e.g. dual-core, quad-core) so that several instructions can be processed in parallel.
Describes memory or storage that keeps its contents without power, e.g. ROM, SSDs and hard discs.
Random access memory: volatile, read/write main memory that holds the operating system, programs and data currently in use.
Read only memory: non-volatile memory that can be read but not normally changed, used to store the boot program.
Part of a storage drive used as extra memory when RAM is full; because storage is much slower than RAM, heavy use slows the computer down.
Describes memory that loses its contents when the power is switched off, e.g. RAM and cache.
The start-up instructions stored in ROM that run when the computer is switched on, checking the hardware and loading the operating system from storage into RAM.
An input device made of a flat pad and a stylus, used to capture freehand drawing or handwritten signatures.
Hardware used to enter data into a computer, e.g. a microphone, mouse, graphics digitiser or touch screen.
A display with a touch-sensitive surface that detects the position of a touch, so it is both an input and an output device.
Software that converts spoken words captured by a microphone into text or commands.
An output device that builds a solid object one thin layer at a time from a computer-aided design (CAD) model, using materials such as plastic, metal or ceramics.
Computer-aided design: software used to design objects on screen; its models can be sent to a 3D printer.
An output device in which a laser forms the page on a drum as a pattern of static charge; toner sticks to the charged areas and is fused onto paper with heat. Fast and high quality.
Hardware used to present information from a computer, e.g. speakers, a printer or a screen.
Non-volatile electronic memory with no moving parts, used in SSDs, USB drives and memory cards.
Magnetic storage with rigid spinning platters divided into tracks and sectors, read and written by moving heads; large capacity at low cost per gigabyte.
High-definition optical discs, such as Blu-ray, read and written by a blue-violet laser; they store far more than a DVD and are used for HD films and games.
Non-volatile storage that uses flash memory chips with no moving parts; faster, more durable, quieter and lower-power than an HDD, but more expensive per gigabyte.
A small removable flash memory card, such as SD or microSD, used to add storage to cameras, phones and games consoles.
A plastic card with an embedded chip that stores a small amount of data and is read by a card reader, e.g. a chip-and-PIN bank card or door entry card.
A small, portable, plug-and-play storage device containing flash memory, connected through a USB port.
How quickly data can be read from or written to a storage device.
The amount of data a storage device can hold, measured in bytes (e.g. GB or TB).
How well a storage device survives knocks, drops, heat and repeated use without losing data.
How easily a storage device can be carried and used in different places, depending on its size and weight.
tips: Write the acronym in full at least once: central processing unit (CPU). Examiners regularly report lost marks for unexplained acronyms.

'Describe the role' means say what it does, with an example if you can: 'the ALU carries out arithmetic such as adding two prices, and logical comparisons such as checking whether a balance is below zero'.
Expand every acronym once in your answer: 'the memory address register (MAR) holds…'. Examiners repeatedly report marks lost for unexpanded acronyms.
In a 4-mark fetch question, one mark usually goes to each of: PC to MAR; instruction into the MDR; copied to the IAR; PC incremented.
Use cause → effect with 'so': 'more cores, so more instructions can be processed at the same time'. A bare 'it's faster' rarely gets the second mark.
For RAM say 'currently in use'; for ROM name the boot program; for cache give both 'faster than RAM' and 'frequently used'.
A full answer names the program (boot program/BIOS), says when it runs (at switch-on), and what it does (checks hardware, loads the OS into RAM).
Learn the table so you can rebuild it from memory: cover a column and test yourself.
Make each point specific to the scenario: not 'it's easy', but 'customers at the kiosk need no training because they just tap pictures of the food'.
Key words that show understanding: 'toner' and 'drum' for laser printers; 'layer by layer' and 'CAD' for 3D printers.
'No moving parts' is the root reason for most SSD advantages – use it, then link it to the scenario.
For 'name and describe two solid-state devices' give the name, what it is like, and a realistic situation where it is used – three ideas for each.
Make every point comparative: 'faster than', 'cheaper per gigabyte than', 'more durable than'.
In 6-mark 'discuss' questions, cover input, output and storage (or each factor asked for), justify each, and finish with a clear recommendation.

6.title: Network technologies
terms: A powerful computer on a network that stores users' files centrally and controls access to them.
Local area network: a network covering a small geographical area, such as one building or site, whose hardware is usually owned by the organisation.
Two or more computers or devices linked by cable or wirelessly so that they can communicate and share resources such as files, printers and software.
A computer that is not connected to a network, so its files, software and devices cannot be shared.
Wide area network: a network covering a large geographical area that uses telecommunications links, such as fibre optic cables or satellites, usually rented from telecoms companies.
The worldwide network of networks: the hardware and connections that carry data between computers around the world. It is the largest WAN.
Everyday physical objects with built-in sensors and connectivity that send and receive data over the internet, such as fitness watches and smart thermostats.
A private network owned by an organisation that uses internet technology but can only be accessed by authorised users who log on.
Uniform resource locator: the unique address of a web page or website, e.g. https://www.nidirect.gov.uk.
A service that uses the internet: a collection of linked web pages stored on web servers and viewed in a browser.
A numerical address given to a device on a network that routers use to send data to the right destination.
A unique hardware address built into every NIC, used by a switch to deliver data to the correct device on a LAN.
A cable, usually copper (e.g. CAT6) or fibre, that physically connects a device's NIC to another device such as a switch.
Network interface card: a circuit board in a computer that lets it connect to a network and provides a port for the network cable.
A device that connects two or more networks, such as a LAN and the internet, and forwards data along the best route using IP addresses.
A device that acts as the central connection point in a LAN and forwards data only to the intended device.
A layout in which all devices are attached to a single backbone cable with a terminator at each end.
When two devices send data on a shared cable at the same time, so the signals interfere and must be resent.
A layout in which each device connects to two others in a closed loop and data travels around it in one direction.
A layout in which each device is connected by its own cable to a central switch (or server).
A device at each end of a bus backbone that absorbs the signal so it does not bounce back along the cable.
The way the devices in a network are arranged and connected.
Fourth-generation mobile technology that provides high-speed wireless data through a network of masts.
Fifth-generation mobile technology with faster speeds, much lower latency and capacity for more devices than 4G, but needing more masts.
The amount of data that can be transmitted in a given time, measured in bits per second (e.g. Mbps).
Short-range, low-power wireless technology that connects two nearby devices directly once they have been paired.
Unwanted signals or obstacles that weaken or corrupt transmitted data.
The delay between data being sent and being received.
Cable made of thin glass strands that carries data as pulses of light, giving very high bandwidth and immunity to electrical interference.
Linking two Bluetooth devices so that they recognise each other and can exchange data.
A device that boosts a signal so that it can travel over longer distances.
Wireless technology that uses radio waves and a wireless router or access point to connect devices to a network without cables.
tips: 'Distinguish between a LAN and a WAN' needs a comparison in each mark: a LAN covers a small area such as one building, whereas a WAN covers a large geographical area. Writing two separate definitions that never compare can lose marks.

Avoid one-word answers such as 'sharing' or 'cheaper'. Say what is shared and why it helps, e.g. 'one laser printer can be shared by all computers, so the organisation does not need to buy a printer for each one'.

Internet versus WWW needs both halves: the internet is the network (hardware and connections) and the WWW is the collection of pages accessed over it. Learn the full expansion 'Internet of Things' and have one example with what it does, e.g. a smart thermostat that lets you switch the heating on from your phone.
When a question shows a bus diagram, name the backbone and say the terminators stop signals reflecting back. For a disadvantage, the classic mark is 'if the backbone fails, the whole network fails'.
Learn one clear feature and one typical use for each technology. Matching questions often pair 'short range, paired devices' with Bluetooth and 'pulses of light through glass' with optical fibre.
'Evaluate' questions reward balance. Give at least one strength and one weakness, link each to a criterion, and finish with a judgement for the situation in the question.
Use comparative words in every point: 'fibre is more secure than wireless because…'. A one-sided description of fibre alone will not get full marks on a compare question.
A justification must use the scenario. 'Fibre is fast' is generic; 'fibre's high bandwidth means the hospital's large scan files arrive in seconds' is justified.

7.title: Cyberspace, network security and data transfer
terms: Using technology to repeatedly harass, track or frighten a person.
Any crime committed using a computer, a network or the internet.
The methods used to protect computers, networks and data from attack, damage or unauthorised access.
Stealing personal or company data, often to sell it or to commit identity fraud.
An attack that floods a server or website with requests so that it cannot respond to genuine users.
Gaining unauthorised access to a computer system or its data, for example to steal, change or delete data.
Using another person's personal details to pretend to be them, for example to obtain credit or goods.
Posting untrue statements online that harm the reputation of a person or an organisation.
Deliberately and falsely altering digital content, such as photos or documents, to deceive.
Emails, texts or websites that pretend to come from a trusted organisation in order to trick people into giving personal details such as passwords or bank details.
Sending bulk unwanted messages, usually adverts or scams, to many people.
Malware that secretly records the keys a user presses and sends the log to a criminal, revealing passwords and card details.
Malicious software designed to damage or disrupt a computer system, or to gain unauthorised access to it or its data.
Software installed secretly that monitors a user's activity and sends the information to a third party.
Malware disguised as useful or legitimate software so that the user installs it; it may delete files or open a back door for hackers.
Self-replicating malware that spreads across a network by itself without needing a host file, using up bandwidth.
Software that scans files, downloads and memory for known malware and quarantines or removes it; it must be updated regularly to recognise new threats.
Turning encrypted data back into readable form using the correct key.
Scrambling data using an algorithm and a key so that it cannot be understood by anyone who does not have the key.
A long password that mixes upper and lower case letters, digits and symbols and is not a dictionary word or personal detail.
A logon that needs two different forms of verification, such as a password and a code sent to a phone.
Permissions linked to a user ID that control what each user can see and do, e.g. no access, read only, read and write.
Hardware or software that monitors and filters data entering or leaving a network, blocking traffic that does not meet security rules.
An access level where a user can view data but cannot change it.
An agreed set of rules governing how data is transmitted between devices.
File Transfer Protocol: rules for uploading and downloading files between computers over a network or the internet.
HyperText Transfer Protocol: rules a browser uses to request web pages from a web server and transfer them.
HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure: HTTP with encryption, so data sent between browser and server cannot be read if intercepted.
tips: For 'describe a threat' give what it is plus its effect. 'DoS is an attack on a website' is weak; 'DoS floods a web server with requests so genuine customers cannot reach it, losing the business sales' earns full marks.
Phishing answers need three ideas for full marks: it pretends to be from a trusted source, it tricks the user, and it aims to obtain personal details such as passwords or bank details.
Examiners say 'malicious software' alone is not enough to define malware. Add what it is designed to do: damage, disrupt or gain unauthorised access.
When asked 'how can malware get onto a computer', give specific routes (email attachment, download from an untrusted website, infected USB stick), not just 'from the internet'.
For encryption, two marks usually need what it does (scrambles data so it is meaningless if intercepted) and who can read it (only someone with the key).
Always link the protection method to the scenario: 'read-only access means pupils can view the timetable but cannot change it'.
'A protocol is a set of rules' gets one mark. For the second, add a detail: what the rules cover (format, error checking) or why they matter (devices from different manufacturers can communicate).
When asked to expand an acronym, spell every word correctly: HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure. For HTTP versus HTTPS the key point is that HTTPS encrypts the data – compare both sides.

8.title: Cloud technology
terms: Storing data and running software on remote servers that are accessed on demand over the internet, instead of on a local computer.
Keeping files on a provider's remote servers so they can be accessed from any device with an internet connection.
A building containing large numbers of servers, with power and cooling, that store data and run cloud services.
A payment model in which an organisation pays only for the cloud resources it actually uses.
A measure of the impact of an organisation's or person's activities on the environment, especially the greenhouse gases they cause.
The ability to increase or decrease storage, bandwidth or users quickly as an organisation's needs change.
A period when a service is unavailable, for example because of an internet failure or provider maintenance.
Playing games that run on remote servers, with video of the game streamed to the player's device over the internet.
Cloud software that lets several people view and edit the same file at the same time, e.g. Google Docs or Microsoft 365.
Keeping copies of a file up to date so that a change made in one place appears on every device and for every user.
A record of the changes made to a file that shows who made them and when, and allows earlier versions to be restored.
tips: A two-mark definition needs two ideas: data or software held on remote servers, and accessed over the internet (on demand). 'Storing stuff online' alone is too vague.
'It is cheaper' earns nothing alone. Say why: 'the organisation does not have to buy and maintain its own servers, so it saves on hardware and technician costs'.
Explain the consequence: 'needs an internet connection, so if the broadband fails staff cannot access their files'. A bare 'needs internet' scores one mark at most.

This topic has been set as a quality of written communication question. Write in full paragraphs, cover producers and players, include drawbacks as well as benefits, and use terms such as latency, streaming and piracy correctly.
When asked about benefits for a team, name the feature and explain the benefit: 'version history lets the team restore an earlier draft if mistakes are made'.

9.title: Ethical, legal and environmental impact
terms: The Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013: protect people who buy at a distance by requiring clear information before payment, giving a 14-day right to cancel most goods and banning hidden extra charges such as pre-ticked boxes.
The 14 days in which a consumer can cancel a distance purchase without giving a reason and receive a refund; for goods it starts the day after delivery.
A contract made without the buyer and seller meeting face to face, e.g. buying online, by phone or by mail order.
The legal right of the creator of an original work to control how it is copied, shared, adapted or sold; in the UK it arises automatically when the work is created.
UK law that protects intellectual property, including software, music, images and text, so that it cannot be copied, shared, sold or adapted without the owner's permission.
Original creative work, such as software, music, designs or writing, that belongs to the person or organisation that created it.
Software whose source code is made available under a licence that allows anyone to view, change and share it, on the conditions the licence sets.
A legal agreement that states how a piece of software may be used, including how many users or computers may run it and for what purpose.
Copying someone else's work or ideas and presenting them as your own.
Illegally copying, downloading, distributing or selling software without the copyright owner's permission.

UK law that makes it a criminal offence to access computer material without permission, to do so in order to commit a further crime, or to carry out unauthorised acts that impair a computer, such as changing or deleting data or spreading malware.
Getting into a computer system, account or data without permission; an offence under section 1 of the Computer Misuse Act 1990.
Someone who gets into a computer system, or the data held on it, without permission.
UK law that updated the UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018, for example requiring organisations to handle data protection complaints and replacing the ICO with the Information Commission.
UK law that works alongside the UK GDPR to control how personal data is collected, stored and used; it replaced the Data Protection Act 1998 and was updated by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025.
The living individual whom the personal data is about.
Any information about a living person who can be identified from it, such as their name, address, photo, email address or an online identifier.
Personal data that needs extra protection because its misuse could cause discrimination or serious harm, e.g. health, religious beliefs, ethnic origin or biometric data.
The UK version of the General Data Protection Regulation, which, with the Data Protection Act 2018, sets the rules for processing personal data in the UK.
The principle that personal data must be adequate, relevant and limited to what is needed for the purpose.
The rules that every organisation must follow when processing personal data, e.g. it must be used for a stated purpose, kept accurate, not kept longer than necessary and kept secure.
A statement telling people what personal data an organisation collects, why, who it is shared with, how long it is kept and what their rights are.
A request by a data subject to see a copy of the personal data an organisation holds about them; normally answered free of charge within one month.
A security incident in which personal data is lost, destroyed, changed or disclosed without authorisation.
The person or organisation that decides why and how personal data is processed and is responsible for complying with data protection law.
A person who advises an organisation on data protection law, trains staff, monitors compliance and is the contact point for the regulator; required for public bodies such as schools.

The independent UK regulator that enforces data protection law, gives guidance, investigates complaints and breaches and can issue fines; it replaced the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) on 30 September 2026.
Rules that employees or pupils agree to that set out how they may use an organisation's computers, network and internet.
Using technology, such as social media or messaging, to repeatedly hurt, threaten or embarrass a particular person.
Websites on encrypted networks that cannot be found with normal search engines and are often used to trade illegal material.
Ideas about what is morally right and wrong; an action can be legal but still unethical.
Deliberately false or misleading information spread online, often made to look like real news.
Deliberately posting provocative or offensive messages online to upset people or start arguments; credited separately from cyberbullying.
Global Positioning System: uses signals from satellites orbiting the Earth to work out the exact location of a device in real time.
A person's right to control information about themselves and to be free from unwanted monitoring or intrusion.
Machines or software carrying out tasks that were previously done by people.
When jobs are lost or changed because digital technology now does work that people used to do.
Using ICT, such as broadband, laptops, cloud apps and video conferencing, to work from home instead of at the workplace.
Training workers in new skills, especially digital skills, so they can keep up with changes in technology.
Pain or injury in the hands, wrists, arms, neck or shoulders caused by repeating the same movements, such as typing or clicking, for long periods.
Designed to fit the user and reduce physical strain, e.g. adjustable chairs, ergonomic keyboards and wrist rests.
tips: If a question asks you to 'name' or 'give the full title' of this law, write the whole title with the year. 'Consumer law' or 'the Consumer Act' earns nothing.
For an 'identify a breach' question, give a specific action ('installing a single-user licence on 20 PCs'), not just the word 'piracy'. Describe questions need the action plus why it breaks the law.

A 3-mark 'describe and relate' answer needs: what it is (1), what it does (1), and the offence it links to under the Computer Misuse Act 1990 (1). Writing 'it is illegal' on its own does not earn the third mark.
Name the law precisely: 'the Data Protection Act 2018' or 'the UK GDPR'. Older mark schemes credit the 1998 Act, but a vague answer such as 'the data law' earns nothing.
When asked to 'state' a principle, write it in full: 'personal data must not be kept for longer than necessary' – not just 'time' or 'storage'. One-word answers rarely earn the mark.
For a 'describe two rights' question, name the right (1) and say what it allows (1). 'The right to see their data by making a subject access request' is a full two-mark point.
Older past papers say 'Information Commissioner' or 'ICO'. Examiners still accept those names, but in your answers today write 'the Information Commission (formerly the ICO)'.
In 'describe a measure' questions, say what the measure is and how it protects the data, e.g. 'encrypt the laptop (1) so if it is stolen the data cannot be read (1)'.
Abbreviations such as 'CMA' or 'CDPA' and missing years can cost the mark in 'name the law' questions. Write out the full title.
Mark schemes credit cyberbullying and trolling as separate points: bullying targets one person repeatedly; trolling tries to provoke anyone. Do not treat them as the same thing.

Questions usually ask for concerns. 'It is bad' earns nothing – say who is affected and how, e.g. 'a person's location can be tracked without consent, which invades their privacy and could allow someone to stalk them'.
Give a specific example for each impact. 'Robots do jobs' is weak; 'robots now paint cars on assembly lines, so fewer paint-shop workers are needed' is a developed point.

Read whether the question asks about the employee or the employer. 'Take a break' is an employee measure; 'provide adjustable chairs' is an employer measure. Answers in the wrong column score nothing.

10.title: Digital applications
terms: An online service from which users find, download and update apps for their device.
A representation of a real object or system, built from data and mathematical rules, that a computer can use to predict how it will behave.
An electronic game played on a console, computer or mobile device, often online with other players.
Information given straight away about how well a user has done, so they can decide what to do next.
A ranked list of players' scores in a game or app, used to motivate people to improve.
A software application designed to run on a smartphone or tablet, usually downloaded from an app store.
Software that uses a computer model, built from data and mathematical rules, to copy how a real object or system behaves so it can be tested or practised safely.
Adding game features such as points, badges and leaderboards to a non-game activity to increase motivation.
A computer-generated 3D environment that the user enters through a headset, and sometimes gloves or controllers, stimulating senses such as sight, hearing and touch.
The UK payment service that moves money between bank accounts almost instantly, usually within seconds.
Using a bank's secure website or app to manage an account, for example viewing statements, paying bills and transferring money.
A feature of online training systems that records each learner's progress, such as modules completed and assessment scores.
Training delivered over the internet, often with multimedia and automatic progress tracking, that learners complete at their own pace.
The buying and selling of goods and services over the internet.
Credit in extended answers for well-organised writing, accurate spelling and grammar, and correct use of specialist terms.
tips: 'Describe a feature' needs the feature and what it does for the user: 'a leaderboard (1) ranks players' scores, which motivates them to improve (1)'.
Always link the feature to the benefit: 'immediate feedback (feature) lets the trainee see straight away what they did wrong, so they improve faster (benefit)'.
In a VR training question, name the hardware (headset, data gloves), explain what the trainee practises, and give a reason it is better than real practice (safety, cost, repetition or feedback).
'Evaluate' means weigh both sides and reach a judgement. 'It's easier' or 'it's faster' on its own earns nothing – say what is faster and why it matters to that person.
If the question asks for advantages to the employer, points like 'learn at your own pace' only earn credit if you link them to the employer, e.g. 'less time away from the shop floor'.
2022 asked only about disadvantages for customers. Underline who the question is about before you start; points about the business would earn nothing.

1.title: Contemporary trends in software development
terms: A paradigm in which the program is a sequence of imperative commands, executed in order and organised into procedures and functions that act on separately stored data.
A style or approach to programming that determines how a solution is structured, e.g. procedural or object-oriented.
A blueprint or template that defines the properties and methods that objects of that type will have.
Keeping an object's data inside the object so that it can only be accessed or changed through the object's own methods.
A variable declared inside a class that holds part of an object's data. Fields are usually private and reached through the class's properties and methods.
Where a new class takes on the properties and methods of an existing class and can add its own.
A procedure or function defined in a class that describes an action an object can carry out.
A single instance created from a class, with its own values for the class's properties.
A paradigm in which a program is built from objects, made from classes, that combine data (properties) with the methods that act on it.
An item of data held by an object, defined in its class.
A marker set in an IDE that pauses execution at a chosen line so the programmer can inspect variable values and step through the code.
An editor feature that lets blocks of code be collapsed and expanded to make long programs easier to navigate.
An IDE tool that lets the programmer pause a program at breakpoints, step through it line by line and watch variable values, to find errors.
Integrated development environment: a single application that provides a code editor, translator, debugger and other tools for developing programs.
An editor feature that suggests or completes keywords, variable and method names as code is typed and shows the parameters a method needs.
The program as written by the programmer in a high-level language, before translation.
An editor feature that displays keywords, strings, comments and other parts of the code in different colours.
A translator that converts the whole of a program into machine code before it is run, producing a separate executable file.
A file of machine code produced by a compiler that can be run without the source code or a translator.
A programming language that uses English-like keywords and is independent of the processor, e.g. C# or Python.
A translator that translates and executes a program one line at a time, without producing an executable file.
The stage of compilation that reads the source code and splits it into tokens such as keywords, names and operators, removing spaces and comments.
Binary instructions that a processor can execute directly.
The machine-code version of a program produced when a compiler translates the source code.
Software that converts source code into machine code, e.g. a compiler or an interpreter.
tips: Examiners reported that answers on procedural programming were often too thin: 'step-by-step instructions' alone is a Level 1 answer. Use the words imperative, sequence, procedures and functions, top-down and data passed as parameters.
Mark schemes credit IntelliSense and auto-complete by name. For 'explain' or 'describe' questions always add the benefit: fewer errors, quicker to write, easier to read or easier to find errors.

2.title: Digital data
terms: The base-2 number system, using only the digits 0 and 1, with each column worth twice the column to its right.
A single binary digit, 0 or 1; the smallest unit of data.
A group of 8 bits; it can store 256 different values (0–255) or one ASCII character.
The base-10 number system, using the digits 0–9, with each column worth ten times the column to its right.
1024 bytes; in the same way a megabyte is 1024 KB, a gigabyte 1024 MB and a terabyte 1024 GB.
American Standard Code for Information Interchange: a character set using 7 bits (128 characters) or 8 bits in extended ASCII (256 characters), mainly for English.
A defined list of characters that a computer recognises, each with its own unique binary code.
The unique number that Unicode gives to a character, for example U+0041 for 'A' (65 in denary).
An international character set that aims to give every character in every writing system, including emoji, a unique code; it uses up to 32 bits per character and its first 128 codes match ASCII.
A variable-length Unicode encoding that stores each character in one to four bytes; ASCII characters use one byte with their ASCII codes, so it is backward compatible with ASCII.
The base-16 number system, using 0–9 and A–F (10–15); one hex digit represents one nibble, so it is used as a shorthand for binary.
A group of 4 bits (half a byte); it can be represented by one hexadecimal digit.
A way of storing a number in which each denary digit is held separately in its own group of four bits, e.g. 47 = 0100 0111.
The leftmost bit of a binary pattern, with the highest place value; in signed methods it shows whether the number is positive (0) or negative (1).
A way of storing a negative number by inverting every bit of the positive number's binary pattern.
A way of storing signed numbers in which the most significant bit is the sign (1 = negative) and the remaining bits give the size of the number.
A way of storing signed whole numbers in which the most significant bit has a negative place value; a negative is formed by inverting the bits of the positive number and adding 1.
The digit passed to the next column on the left when a column total in binary addition is 2 or more.
When the result of a calculation is too large to be stored in the number of bits available, so the extra bit is lost and the stored result is wrong.
A data type with only two possible values, true or false.
A data type for a single letter, digit or symbol.
The kind of value a variable holds, which determines how much memory it uses and which operations can be carried out on it.
A data type for storing a date and/or a time, allowing date calculations and formatting.
A data type for whole numbers, positive or negative, with no fractional part.
A data type for numbers that have a fractional (decimal) part.
A data type that holds a sequence of characters (letters, digits, symbols, spaces) written inside quotation marks.
An operator that combines or reverses Boolean values: AND (true only if both inputs are true), OR (true if at least one is true) and NOT (reverses the input).
A table showing the output of a Boolean expression for every possible combination of inputs.
tips: If asked to 'describe how a number is converted to a binary pattern', explain the idea: write the place values (doubling from 1), place a 1 under each value used to make the number and a 0 elsewhere, and give a worked example such as 54 = 00110110.
Calculation questions give marks for method. Write the conversion step (× 1024 or ÷ 1024) before the answer, and state the unit of your final answer.

For 'describe two differences', give two different points, e.g. range of characters/languages and bits/storage per character. Writing one difference twice the other way round ('ASCII has fewer, Unicode has more') scores once.
Write all eight bits, including the leading zeros, when a question asks for an 8-bit or one-byte answer. Then check by adding the place values back up: it takes ten seconds and catches most slips.
For 'give an advantage of hexadecimal', compare it with binary: shorter / easier for humans to read and remember, so fewer errors. Saying 'it uses less memory' is wrong and earns nothing.
To check a two's complement answer, add up the place values with the MSB counted as −128. If you used the invert-and-add-1 method and the check does not match, you probably forgot to add the 1.

Show your carries above or below the columns: they earn working marks. When asked to 'explain overflow', give both parts: the result is too big for the number of bits available and the extra bit is lost, so the answer stored is wrong.
Justify a data type by linking it to the data, not just naming it: 'real, because the cost includes pence' or 'Boolean, because equipment is either hired or not'.
Fill in every row, including the working columns. Many lost marks come from a single wrong row in an intermediate column carried into the output.

3.title: Digital design principles
terms: Removing or hiding details of a problem that are not needed to solve it, so the focus is on what is important.
A precise, step-by-step set of instructions that solves a problem.
An approach to solving problems so that a computer can help, using ideas such as decomposition and abstraction to produce an algorithm.
Breaking a large, complex problem down into smaller, more manageable sub-problems that can be solved separately.
Spotting similarities, repeated steps or trends in a problem or its data, so that one solution can be reused for several parts.
Designing a solution by breaking the main task into sub-tasks, and those into smaller sub-tasks, often shown as a structure diagram.
A diagram that represents an algorithm using standard symbols for start/stop, input/output, process and decision, joined by flow lines.
A control structure in which a block of statements is repeated, using a loop such as FOR or WHILE.
A language-independent, structured English-like way of writing an algorithm using programming-style keywords.
A control structure in which a condition is tested to decide which statements are executed, e.g. IF … ELSE.
A control structure in which statements are executed one after another in the order they are written.
A sort that repeatedly passes through a list comparing adjacent items and swapping them if they are in the wrong order, until a pass makes no swaps.
In a sort, swapping the positions of two items; the number of exchanges is one measure of a sorting algorithm's efficiency.
One complete sweep through a list during a sorting algorithm.
A sorting algorithm that keeps items with equal values in the same order relative to each other as they were before the sort.
A sort that builds a sorted section at the start of the list by taking each next item and inserting it into its correct position.
The number giving an element's position in an array or a character's position in a string; in C# indexes start at 0.
A search that checks each item in turn from the start until the target is found or the end of the list is reached.
A search of a sorted list that repeatedly checks the middle item and discards the half that cannot contain the target.
In a binary search, the part of the list (from the first to the last position still being considered) that could still contain the target; it halves after each comparison.
Improving a design in stages, for example after dry runs or user feedback, by adding missing steps, correcting logic or simplifying it.
A simple sketch of a screen layout showing where prompts, input boxes, buttons and messages will go, used to plan an interface and get user feedback.
A table describing each data item in a solution, e.g. its name, purpose, data type, example value and validation rule.
The items of data a solution needs (inputs, processed and stored values, outputs), each with its name, data type and validation.
Checking an algorithm or code by hand, without running it on a computer, to find errors.
Working through an algorithm or program by hand, line by line, recording the values of variables to check its logic and output.
A table used in a dry run to record the value of each variable, condition and output at each step.
tips: In the 6-mark extended question, for each concept give a definition, an example in the context of the question, and a benefit. Answers that only define the terms stay in the lowest level.

Algorithm-writing questions carry more marks than anything else on the paper. Follow every bullet point in the question, use the variable names given, and close every IF and loop clearly (END IF, END WHILE, NEXT).
When asked to show a bubble sort, write out the whole list after each pass. If asked how the algorithm knows it has finished, the answer is: a complete pass with no swaps.

In the extended question on the two sorts, describe each method in steps first, then compare them on efficiency (number of comparisons, nearly sorted data) and simplicity. A comparison with no description cannot reach the top level.
A complete description of a linear search mentions the start (first item), the comparison with the target, moving to the next item, and both stopping conditions: found, or end of list.
The condition for a binary search, the list must be sorted, is asked for almost every time. When tracing, write down the low, high and middle positions at each step.
If a question asks how a design could be refined, give a specific improvement and why it helps, e.g. 'add a range check on age so impossible values are rejected before the price is calculated'.
If asked to design or evaluate an interface, link each feature to the user in the scenario: 'a drop-down list for pitch size means the user cannot type an invalid size'.
When asked how a dry run helps, give two separate points, e.g. it finds logic errors and it checks the expected output is produced. Examiners noted many answers made only one point.

4.title: Programming constructs
terms: A named value that is set once and cannot be changed while the program is running.
The name given to a variable, constant, array or subroutine so that it can be referred to in the code; it should be meaningful.
A named location in memory that stores a value which can change while the program is running.
A symbol that performs a calculation: + (add), − (subtract), * (multiply), / (divide), DIV, MOD and ^ (power).
Integer division: gives the whole-number part of a division and discards any remainder, e.g. 17 DIV 5 = 3. In C#, / between two ints.
Modulus: gives the remainder after division, e.g. 17 MOD 5 = 2. In C# the operator is %.
A comparison operator that gives True or False: = (== in C#), ≠ (!=), <, >, <= and >=.
A statement that stores a value, or the result of an expression, in a variable (← in pseudocode, = in C#).
A statement that takes data from the user (e.g. the keyboard) and stores it in a variable; in C#, Console.ReadLine().
A statement that displays data or results to the user, e.g. on screen with Console.WriteLine().
A data structure that stores a fixed number of values of the same data type under a single identifier, each accessed by its index.
One individual value stored in an array.
Joining two or more strings together end to end to make one string; + in C#.
A built-in function or method that works with text, e.g. Length, Substring, IndexOf, Contains, Split, ToUpper.
A part of a string; in C#, Substring(start, length) extracts length characters beginning at index start.
An IF statement placed inside another IF statement, so the inner condition is only tested if the outer condition is True.
A loop that repeats until (or while) a condition is met, so the number of repetitions is not known in advance, e.g. WHILE or REPEAT…UNTIL.
A loop that repeats a fixed, known number of times, e.g. a FOR loop.
A loop that never ends because its terminating condition can never be met.
A loop that tests its condition after each repetition, so the body always runs at least once (REPEAT…UNTIL; do…while in C#).
A loop that tests its condition before each repetition, so the body may run zero times (WHILE).
A variable, initialised to 0 before a loop, to which each value is added inside the loop.
A special input value, such as −1 or 0, that signals the end of the data and stops a loop.
A function provided by the programming language or its libraries, e.g. Math.Round or Convert.ToInt32, that the programmer can call without writing it.
A subroutine that performs a task and returns a single value to the code that called it.
A variable in a subroutine's definition that receives a value (argument) passed in when the subroutine is called.
A subroutine that performs a task but does not return a value (void in C#).
A named, self-contained block of code that performs a specific task and can be called whenever it is needed.
Opening, reading from, writing to, appending to and closing files so that data is stored permanently between runs of a program.
A collection of related fields about one item; in a text file, usually one line with fields separated by commas.
tips: To decide whether a value should be a constant, ask: 'Could this change while one run of the program is happening?' A price list or a conversion rate – constant. A user's input, a counter or a total – variable.
n MOD 2 = 0 is the standard test for an even number. MOD is also used to check whether one number divides exactly into another.

In algorithm questions, use the variable names given in the question and remember the final OUTPUT statement – it is usually worth a mark of its own. Write calculations with variable names (total ← nights * hireCost), not with the numbers from the example.

In 'complete the algorithm' questions the marks usually sit on the loop limits, the comparison between neighbours (list[j] > list[j + 1]) and the three-line exchange through a temporary variable. Write all three lines of the exchange; list[j] = list[j + 1] on its own loses a value.

In 'write a search' questions, marks go for: starting at index 0, a loop that stops at the end of the array, comparing the element with the target, a found flag (or return), and an output for both found and not found.

When a question asks you to 'name a string function and describe its use', give the name, what it returns and an example from the scenario, e.g. 'Length returns the number of characters in the password, so it can check there are at least 8'.

If a question says use only one condition in each IF, obey it: write separate IFs such as IF numPupils < 20 THEN … END IF and IF numPupils >= 20 THEN … END IF. Tick off every bullet point in the question – each one usually maps to a mark.
For 'two advantages' questions give two different benefits, each with a reason – 'easier to test because each function can be tested separately' is better than 'easier'.
'Name two file handling functions other than read and write': open, close, append, delete, or check a file exists – and describe what each does in one sentence.

5.title: Simple error handling techniques
terms: A validation check that makes sure data matches a required pattern, e.g. an email address containing @.
A validation check that makes sure the number of characters entered is acceptable, e.g. a password of at least 8 characters.
A validation check that makes sure data has been entered and a field has not been left blank.
A validation check that makes sure a value lies between a lower and an upper limit.
A validation check that makes sure data is of the correct data type, e.g. a whole number rather than text.
An automatic check carried out by a program to make sure input data is sensible, reasonable and follows set rules before it is processed; it cannot guarantee the data is correct.
A loop (usually WHILE) that repeats the input, with an error message, for as long as the data entered is invalid.
An error that occurs while the program is running and causes it to crash, e.g. dividing by zero or opening a file that does not exist.
An error in the program's reasoning that lets it run without crashing but produces incorrect results.
An error where the code breaks the grammar rules of the programming language, so it cannot be translated and the program will not run.
Code that detects a run-time error (exception) and handles it, e.g. with try … catch, so the program displays a helpful message instead of crashing.
An error event raised (thrown) by a program when something goes wrong at run time, such as a FormatException or DivideByZeroException.
tips: In 'write a validation loop' questions, marks usually go for: the first input, a correct WHILE condition (watch AND vs OR), an error message inside the loop, re-input inside the loop, and the right variable names from the question.

In 6-mark quality-of-written-communication questions, cover each error type with a definition, an example and how it is detected and dealt with. Use the technical terms – exception, trace table, breakpoint, test data.
A full answer to 'describe error trapping' says what it is (detecting a run-time error), how (try … catch) and what happens instead of a crash (a message, recovery).

6.title: Developing test plans and testing a solution
terms: Testing that checks the outputs produced for given inputs against the requirements, without looking at the code; often done by independent testers or users.
Testing that separately developed modules work correctly together, including the data passed between them.
Testing carried out repeatedly throughout development and after it: each part is tested, errors are fixed and the tests are repeated until the part works.
Testing the complete, integrated system as a whole against its specification and requirements.
Testing a single module, function or method on its own to check that it works correctly before it is combined with others.
Testing that examines the internal code, logic and structure of a program so that every path and condition is executed; usually done by the programmer.
The precise result that should happen when a test is carried out, written before the test is run so it can be compared with the actual outcome.
Measurable statements, based on the user requirements, that a solution must meet to be judged successful.
A planned table of tests showing, for each test, its number, purpose, test data, type of data, expected outcome, actual outcome and any action taken.
Valid test data on the limits (boundaries) of the accepted range, which should be accepted.
