Test data that breaks the rules, e.g. outside the accepted range or of the wrong type, which the program should reject.
A test in which no data is entered, to check that a blank input is rejected or handled.
Typical, sensible test data within the accepted range that the program should accept and process.
tips: 'Describe two differences between black and white box testing' – make each difference a contrast: 'white box looks at the code, whereas black box only considers inputs and outputs'.
In Unit 5, moderators often find extreme data and the action/retest column missing. Include tests on every boundary and record what you changed.
Always state the type and say why: '16 – extreme, because it is the lowest age the gym accepts'.

7.title: Evaluation of digitally authored systems
terms: Judging how well a solution meets the original user requirements and design criteria, using evidence such as test results and user feedback, and identifying improvements.
A requirement that states something the system must be able to do, such as calculate a total or produce a report.
A requirement that states how the system should work rather than what it does, such as its response time, usability, reliability or platform.
People with an interest in a system, such as the client, the end users and the developers.
The agreed list of what a system must do, drawn up with the client at the start of a project and used to judge the finished solution.
A solution that carries out its tasks quickly without wasting resources (processor time, memory, storage) or the user's time and effort.
Testing a system with a large quantity of data to check that it still performs correctly and does not fail.
The ability of a solution to cope with invalid, unexpected or extreme data and high volumes of data without crashing or giving wrong results.
tips: Be evaluative, not descriptive. 'The program has a menu' earns little; 'Requirement 3 is fully met – all four menu options worked in tests 4–7' earns credit.

For 'how could robustness be tested?', refer to at least two kinds of data (e.g. invalid and high volumes) and say what result would show the system is robust – it rejects the bad data with a message and does not crash.

1.title: Reasons for systems development
terms: A smaller system that forms part of a larger system, performing one part of its overall function and usually exchanging data with other sub-systems.
A set of interdependent components that work together to achieve a defined purpose and meet a defined need.
Raw facts and figures that have no context or meaning on their own, input to or stored by a system.
Data that has been processed and given context so that it has meaning and can be used, e.g. in a report or alert.
An operation carried out by a computer system that manipulates data, such as calculating, validating, sorting, searching or updating, to turn data into information.
The means by which a user interacts with a computer system: it allows the user to enter data and to view the results of processing.
How easily, efficiently and satisfactorily the intended users can use a system to carry out their tasks.
A combination of people, procedures, hardware, software and data that collects, processes, stores and distributes information to support an organisation.
An old system that is still in use but is often unreliable, unsupported by its supplier or expensive to maintain.
The period from the mid-1960s when software projects were frequently late, over budget, unreliable and failed to meet user requirements, because development methods could not keep pace with demand.
The application of a disciplined, systematic (engineering) approach to the design, development and maintenance of software.
A structured framework of stages – feasibility, analysis, design, development, testing, implementation, maintenance and evaluation – used to plan, build and maintain an information system.
The end product of a stage of development, such as the system specification or design document, which is passed on as the input to the next stage.
A limit within which a system must be developed or operate, such as the budget, the deadline, available hardware or legislation.
The requirements that an organisation and the individuals who use a system have of it: what it must do and how they need to interact with it.
Whether the expected benefits of a proposed system outweigh its costs, usually assessed with a cost–benefit analysis.
A preliminary investigation to decide whether a proposed system is technically, economically, legally, operationally and schedule feasible, ending in a recommendation on whether to proceed.
Whether a proposed system can be developed and operated in compliance with relevant law, such as data protection, computer misuse and copyright legislation.
Whether a proposed system will work in practice within the organisation and be accepted and used by its staff and customers.
Whether a proposed system can be developed and implemented by the date it is required.
Whether the hardware, software, network capacity and technical skills needed to build and run the proposed system exist and are available.
A comparison of the estimated one-off and ongoing costs of a proposed system with its expected tangible and intangible benefits over a period of time.
The document produced by a feasibility study, setting out the problem, the options considered, their feasibility and a justified recommendation for management.
A benefit of a system that is difficult to measure in money, such as improved customer satisfaction or staff morale.
The length of time it takes for the cumulative benefits of a system to equal its cumulative costs.
A benefit of a system that can be measured in money, such as reduced staffing or postage costs.
The person who writes, comments, tests and debugs the source code for the system designed by the systems analyst, and writes its operational documentation.
The person responsible for planning, scheduling, resourcing, monitoring and managing risk so that a project is delivered on time, within budget and to the required quality.
The person who identifies the user and data processing requirements of a new or modified system, carrying out the feasibility study and fact-finding and producing the system specification.
tips: If asked to identify the three characteristics for a given system, apply each one to the scenario: a purpose written as 'to…', a need written as the problem it solves, and at least two named components. Generic definitions alone usually earn only the first mark.

'Explain the choice of interface' questions are usually marked as factor + justification pairs. Name the factor (application, environment or user), then link it to a specific feature of the scenario: 'the kiosk is used by the public with no training (user), so it needs large buttons and few steps (1+1)'.

A strong answer links the need to a consequence: 'customers must find it easy to book, otherwise they will book with a competitor, so the company loses income and the system fails its purpose' is worth more than 'it must be easy to use'.
Questions often ask for 'reasons' and 'impact' separately. Give a cause, then its consequence: 'there was little past experience, so time and cost estimates were inaccurate and projects overran'.

Explain the effect of each factor on development, not just its name. 'Cost – the budget limits how many programmers can be employed, so fewer features can be built' earns two marks; 'cost – how much it costs' earns none.

Name the criterion, then apply it to the scenario: 'Operational – the reception staff have little IT experience, so they may resist the system unless they are trained (2)'. A textbook definition of 'economic' alone rarely scores.
In a calculation, set out a year-by-year table with a cumulative row. Method marks are often available even if an arithmetic slip spoils the final figure.
Role questions are usually '1 mark for the main role + 1 mark per duty'. Learn a one-line main role for each, then at least four duties.

2.title: Analysis
terms: The stage of systems development in which the existing system is investigated and the requirements of the new system are identified and agreed with the client.
Gathering information about a current system, using techniques such as interviews, questionnaires, observation and document sampling, to establish how it works and what is required.
The document produced at the end of analysis that states precisely what the client expects the system to do, including its requirements, constraints and schedule, and is agreed by the client.
A source of data collected first-hand specifically for the current purpose, such as a questionnaire designed for the project.
Data that already exists and is reused for a purpose other than the one for which it was originally collected.
A question with a fixed set of possible answers, producing quantitative data that is easy to analyse.
A question that lets the respondent answer in their own words, giving richer qualitative data that is harder to analyse.
An interview with a fixed set of questions asked in the same order to every interviewee, making answers easy to compare.
Examining a sample of existing forms, invoices, reports and records to identify the users, data items, formats, data flows, volumes and outputs of the current system.
The tendency of people to change their behaviour because they know they are being observed, which can make observation unrepresentative.
Checking a finding from one source of evidence against another to confirm that it is accurate and consistent.
A person who operates a system directly, in their day-to-day work or as a customer.
A method of prioritising requirements as Must have, Should have, Could have and Won't have this time.
A person or group with an interest in a system or who is affected by it, such as managers, end users, customers, suppliers and regulators.
A statement of something the system must do or allow its users to do, such as an input, process, calculation or output.
A condition or constraint on how the system behaves – such as response time, availability, reliability, security or usability – rather than a function it performs.
A measurable characteristic used to judge a system, such as performance, reliability or security; non-functional requirements specify these.
A requirement stated precisely enough, usually with a measure, that it can be shown to have been met or not.
The documented statements of what the users and client need the new system to do (functional requirements) and how well it must do it (non-functional requirements), agreed during analysis.

An approach to development, based on the 2001 Agile Manifesto, that delivers working software early and incrementally in short iterations, with close customer collaboration and acceptance of changing requirements.
An agreed process for requesting, assessing, approving and recording changes to a system's requirements during a project.
A diagram that models how data moves through a system using external entities, processes, data stores and labelled data flows.
A labelled arrow on a DFD showing data moving between external entities, processes and data stores.
A place on a DFD where data is held for later use, such as a file or database table, given a unique identifier such as D1.
An activity on a DFD that transforms input data into output data; it is named with a verb phrase and given a unique number.
A person, organisation or system outside the system boundary that supplies data to the system or receives data from it.
An external entity that receives data from the system.
An external entity that supplies data to the system.
The top-level (Level 0) DFD, showing the whole system as a single process with its external entities and the data flows between them, defining the system boundary.
The rule that the data flows into and out of a process, or the whole system, must be the same on its exploded lower-level DFD.
To break a DFD process down into more detailed sub-processes on a lower-level diagram.
A DFD in which the single process of the context diagram is exploded into its main numbered sub-processes, with data stores and internal flows added.
An error on a DFD where a process has inputs but no outputs.
tips: For 'describe the purpose of analysis', mark schemes typically credit: understand inputs/processes/outputs of the existing system (1), identify strengths and weaknesses (1), identify opportunities for improvement or new features (1), establish/agree the user requirements (1).
When asked for the 'main features' of a technique, describe how it is carried out (who, how, what is recorded), not just its advantages.
Name the Hawthorne effect when evaluating observation – and explain it: staff who know they are watched may 'act up' and work differently from normal, so the analyst sees an unrepresentative picture.
In 6–8 mark discussions, cover several techniques, give strengths and weaknesses applied to the scenario, and finish with a reasoned recommendation of the best combination.
A 3-mark scenario answer typically needs: the technique (1), who it would be used with (1), and a justification linked to the scenario (1).
When describing a stakeholder's needs, keep it specific to the scenario – 'reception staff need to check in a patient in under 30 seconds' rather than 'users want it easy'.

A typical 2-mark 'distinguish' answer: functional describes an action/task the system must carry out (1); non-functional is a condition, constraint or quality the system must meet, such as response time or security (1).
If asked to name the document produced at the end of analysis, write 'system (requirements) specification'. 'Design specification' is the deliverable of the design stage.

A full answer gives the old role (binding, two-way contract), the reasons it worked (few vendors, predictable planning), and the two reasons for change (more suppliers/skills; Agile iterative development).
The four purpose points above match those credited in mark schemes – learn them as a list.
If a department is inside the system being modelled, it may appear as a process rather than an entity. Always check what the question says the system covers.

Context-diagram marks are typically one for the single correctly named process, one per correct entity and one per correctly labelled flow in the right direction. Unlabelled arrows usually score nothing.

Asked about the relationship between the levels? Say: Level 1 shows the context diagram in more detail, exploding the single process into sub-processes; it adds data stores; and it keeps the same external flows (consistency).
When identifying an error, name the rule broken and give a specific correction – most mark schemes award a mark for each.

3.title: System design, development and testing
terms: A central record of every data item in a system, giving its name, description, data type, length, format, validation rule, example value and key status.

The deliverable of the design stage, setting out the user interface and navigation, input and output design, data structures and data dictionary, validation and verification, algorithms, security and an initial test plan for the new system.
The routes a user takes between the screens or pages of a system, e.g. which button or link leads to which screen.

A design technique in which each screen of a proposed interface is sketched as a frame showing its contents and inputs/outputs, with arrows for the navigation between screens, so users can give feedback before coding.
A description of the data a system holds – its tables (entities), their fields and the relationships between them.
The appearance and behaviour of an interface as experienced by a user – its layout, colours, menus and how it responds.
Building an early, incomplete working version of a system so that users can experience its look and feel and give feedback on the interface and on the data the system needs.
A part of a prototype or program, such as a menu option or subroutine, that is present but has no working functionality yet.
The study and design of how people interact with computer systems, so that interfaces are usable, efficient, error-resistant and accessible.
Deciding what data a system captures, the method of capture and the layout of input screens or forms.
Deciding the content, format and medium of a system’s screens, reports and documents to suit their audience.
A way of organising a collection of related data items under one identifier so that they can be stored and processed efficiently.
An extra digit calculated from the other digits of a code and appended to it, recalculated on entry to detect keying errors.
A validation check that compares two or more fields to make sure their values are compatible, e.g. a return date after a loan date.
A validation check that data matches a required pattern of characters, e.g. a postcode or car registration.
A validation check that a value matches one of a list of allowed values.
A validation check that a required field has not been left blank.
A validation check that a value lies between a lower and an upper limit.
An automatic check by the system that data is reasonable and obeys set rules before it is accepted; it cannot ensure the data is correct.
A check that data has been entered or transferred accurately, i.e. it matches the original, for example by double entry or a visual check.
The final test, by the client’s end users in their live environment with genuine data at realistic volumes, to confirm the system meets their requirements before they sign it off.
The final phase of in-house testing carried out by the developer, following a test plan, before the software is released to users.
Testing of a pre-release version by a group of potential external users in a realistic environment, without developers present, who report any faults.
An error that appears only when separately tested units are joined, usually because of inconsistent data at the interface between them.
Testing units that have already been tested once they are combined, to check they work together and pass data between them correctly.
Testing the complete, integrated system against its agreed specification, following a test plan; essentially black-box testing of the whole system.
Testing an individual module or subroutine on its own, usually in-house by the programmer, to check it works correctly in all circumstances.
Testing that compares actual outputs with expected outputs for given inputs, without any access to or knowledge of the program code.
Testing that uses knowledge of the program code to design tests that exercise every path, branch and loop.
Formal agreement by the client or manager that a stage's deliverable is complete and accepted, allowing the next stage to begin.
The precise result a test should produce if the system is working correctly, written before the test is run.
A document listing every test to be carried out, giving the part of the system tested, what is being tested, the test data and the expected outcome, with space for the actual outcome and pass/fail.
Valid test data at the very edges of an allowed range, used to detect errors in range limits.
Test data that is wrong in type, format or range and should be rejected by the system.
Typical valid test data, correct in type and format, that the system should accept and process.
tips: A four-mark ‘list the contents of a design document’ question wants four different, specific items, e.g. ‘design of input screens’ and ‘validation required for each field’. Vague answers such as ‘how the system works’ score nothing.
Questions often ask how prototyping is used for the interface and the data model. Answer both parts separately – many candidates forget the data model.

In design questions, name the feature and explain how it helps the user, e.g. ‘a drop-down list of class names prevents spelling errors, so records match’. A feature with no justification usually earns only half the credit.
‘Range check’ on its own often earns half the credit. Write ‘range check: the age must be a whole number from 11 to 19 inclusive’.
‘Why is testing important?’ – give distinct reasons: meets the user requirements, finds errors before live use, cheaper to fix early, gives the client confidence before acceptance.
When asked for the main components, the four the mark scheme looks for are: the part of the system tested, what is being tested, the test data, and the expected outcome.

4.title: System implementation
terms: The process of moving from an old system to a new one using a planned method: parallel, direct, pilot or phased.
Transferring existing data into the format and structure the new system requires, e.g. keying in or scanning paper records, then verifying and validating them.

The stage at which a new system is put into operation in place of the old one, including installing hardware and software, converting data, training users, providing documentation and managing the changeover.
A changeover method in which the old system stops and the new one takes over at a single moment, with no overlap.
A changeover method in which the old and new systems run at the same time on the same transactions so that outputs can be compared until the new system is proven.
A changeover method in which the new system is introduced one component or function at a time until the whole system is in use.
A changeover method in which the whole new system is introduced in one branch, department or site before being extended to the rest of the organisation.
Moving data from an old computer system into a new one, often with reformatting and specialist conversion software.
A training method in which a small number of staff are trained and then train their colleagues.
Training delivered electronically, such as online modules or video tutorials, that users complete at their own pace.
The written and diagrammatic record produced at each stage of development, and for the finished system, describing what it does and how it works and is used.

Documentation for administrators and maintenance staff, including the specification, data models, input/output and report designs, annotated code, test plans and results, and hardware/software configuration.
Non-technical documentation for end users, such as an overview, installation instructions, a user guide, troubleshooting, FAQs, training materials and backup procedures.
Program code that includes comments explaining its purpose and logic, so that others can understand and maintain it.
Frequently asked questions: a section of user documentation answering common queries.
A section of user documentation explaining what to do when problems occur, including the meaning of error messages.
Part of the user documentation giving step-by-step instructions, usually with screenshots, for carrying out common tasks.
Any change applied to a system during its lifespan after it has been implemented.
Changes made so that a system can still carry out its tasks after an internal or external change in circumstances, such as new legislation, a new tax rate or a new business policy.
Changes made to fix flaws, errors or weaknesses, including security flaws, found after the system is in use.
An ongoing agreement under which a developer maintains a system for a client in return for regular payment.
Changes that improve the performance, efficiency or usability of a system that already works.
A small piece of software released to fix, update or improve a program or its data, often downloaded and installed automatically.
The measures used to judge a system after implementation, such as effectiveness, efficiency, usability, reliability and cost–benefit.
A formal evaluation, after a system has been in use for some time, of how well it meets its original objectives and requirements, recommending further maintenance and recording lessons learned.
tips: If asked for the purpose of implementation, mention both what (making the new system operational and replacing the old) and how (resources, data conversion, training, changeover).
Structure: name the method (1), link a feature of the scenario to a benefit (1), and, for full marks, say why an alternative is less suitable (1).
In a scenario question, name the actual records (e.g. the diary, receipt book) and say what tables they become in the new system.
‘Evaluate’ means advantages and disadvantages applied to the scenario, ending with a judgement.
Give different reasons, each in a sentence. ‘To help people’ is too vague to score.
‘User documentation tells you how to use the system’ is worth at most one mark. List specific components, each different.

5.title: Alternative development approaches
terms: A structured framework of stages, roles, techniques and documents used to organise the development of an information system, such as the waterfall model, RAD or Agile.

A sequential development methodology in which distinct stages (analysis, design, implementation, testing, maintenance) are completed in order, each producing a deliverable and being signed off before the next stage begins.
The point at which work passes from one waterfall stage, often from one group of staff to another; misunderstandings introduced here may travel undetected through later stages.
A working addition to a product delivered at the end of an iteration or sprint, so that the system grows step by step.
An approach in which a system is built through repeated cycles of planning, design, coding and testing, each producing a working version that users review to shape the next cycle.
Identifying possible threats to a project's success, assessing their likelihood and impact, and deciding how to reduce or resolve them.
A risk-driven iterative model, proposed by Barry Boehm, in which each loop determines objectives, identifies and resolves risks, develops and tests the next version, and plans the next loop.
An approach in which a prototype is repeatedly refined in response to user feedback until it becomes the final system.
An early model of all or part of a system, built quickly so that users can evaluate it and clarify their requirements.
An approach in which a prototype is used to establish and agree requirements and is then discarded before the real system is built.
The final phase of RAD, in which the new system replaces the old, involving final testing, data conversion, changeover and training.

A methodology that delivers systems quickly through a series of builds and four phases (requirements planning, user design, construction, cutover), with frequent prototypes, continual user involvement and a strict timescale with prioritised requirements.
Fixing the time allowed for a project or part of it so that the deadline cannot be overrun; lower-priority features are dropped instead.
In Agile, the prioritised wish list of all the features the product should eventually provide, maintained by the product owner.
The Scrum team member who acts as the voice of the client, setting priorities in the backlogs and preventing unrealistic items being added.
In Agile, the features selected from the product backlog for the next release, broken down into estimated, prioritised work items.
A framework for running an Agile project in fixed-length sprints, with a Scrum master, product owner and multi-skilled team working as one unit.
The team member responsible for ensuring the Scrum team works effectively: arranging meetings, monitoring progress and removing obstacles.
A small, multi-skilled team (developers, testers and customer input led by a Scrum master with a product owner) able to analyse, design, build and test the software.
In Agile, a fixed period of a few weeks (no more than a month) in which the team produces a working increment of the product.
A meeting at the end of a sprint in which the team reflects on its process and agrees improvements for the next sprint.
A meeting at the end of a sprint in which the completed work is inspected and presented to the product owner.
A graph of the work remaining in a sprint against time, compared with an ideal straight line, used to check whether work is on schedule.
A short daily meeting of about 15 minutes in which each team member says what they did yesterday, what they will do today and what obstacles they face.
A relative unit used by Agile teams to estimate the effort needed for a backlog item.
Merging all developers' code into a shared version frequently, with an automatic build and test run each time, so integration problems are found quickly.
An Agile method focused on engineering practices such as pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration, refactoring and small frequent releases.
An extreme programming practice in which two programmers work at one computer, one writing code and the other reviewing it, swapping roles regularly.
Improving the internal structure of existing code without changing its external behaviour.
A practice in which an automated test is written before the code, and just enough code is then written to make the test pass.
tips: For a 'describe the main features' question, four separate points usually earn the marks: distinct stages in sequence; each completed before the next; a deliverable from each stage; going back if an error is found. Naming the five stages on its own counts as only one point.

If a question asks you to compare user involvement, contrast waterfall (start and end only) with RAD (continual, through prototypes) and Agile (constant consultation; the product owner represents the client throughout).

Disadvantages score more when you explain the consequence: not just 'inflexible', but 'if the client's needs change after design is signed off, the project must return to the design stage, adding cost and delay'.

In 'describe the users' involvement in RAD' questions, the key phrase is continual involvement through frequent prototypes, so errors are identified early. Contrast this with waterfall's start-and-end involvement if the question invites comparison.
If you are given a burn down chart, quote figures: 'on day 4, 42 points remained against an ideal of 36, so the team was 6 points behind'. Precise readings earn marks that vague descriptions do not.
Phrases such as 'because the scenario says...' keep your answer applied. Generic lists of features with no link to the context score poorly in extended questions, however accurate they are.

6.title: Software projects
terms: A resource whose amount can be increased or decreased, such as the budget or number of staff; an inelastic resource, such as time before a hard deadline, cannot be changed.
Anything a project can use to meet its objectives: human (e.g. programmers), technical (e.g. processing power), financial (the budget) or physical (e.g. accommodation).
Changes to what the client wants after the project has started, often caused by inadequate user involvement during analysis, leading to rework, delay and extra cost.
Anything that could have a harmful effect on a project or cause it to fail, such as missed deadlines, requirements shift, staff turnover or low productivity.
A measurable value (metric), such as time taken, error rate or user satisfaction, used to judge whether an objective has been met.
Objectives that are Specific, Measurable, Agreed, Realistic and Timed, so that all parties share the same view of what counts as success.
A horizontal bar chart showing project tasks against a timeline, including their start and end, duration, overlaps, dependencies and milestones.
A significant point in a project, such as the sign-off of a deliverable, used to check progress against the plan.
The longest sequence of dependent tasks through a project, which determines its minimum duration; any delay to a task on it delays the whole project.
A project-planning technique that models tasks as a network of nodes (events) and arrows (tasks) to find earliest start and latest finish times, the critical path and float.
In critical path analysis, the earliest time a task can start, once every task it depends on has finished.
The amount of time a non-critical task can be delayed without delaying the completion of the whole project; float = LFT − EST − duration.
In critical path analysis, the latest time by which an activity must be complete if the project is not to be delayed.
The central store in which a version management system holds all of a project's files and their complete history of changes.
The process by which a development team keeps track of changes to code files over time, recording who made each change, when and why, and allowing return to earlier versions.
In version management, a separate line of development used to work on a feature or fix without affecting the main version.
Saving a change to the repository as a new version, together with a note describing the change.
Combining two parallel versions or branches into a single version that contains both sets of changes.
Returning to an earlier, stable version of the code and continuing development from that point, discarding later faulty changes.
A diagram of a file's history in which nodes are versions and arrows show which version each was created from, showing parallel versions, merges and rollbacks.
Computer-aided software engineering tool: software that supports or automates parts of development, such as diagramming (upper CASE) or code generation and debugging (lower CASE).
Software that helps a development team co-ordinate its work, such as shared repositories and issue trackers, messaging, video meetings, shared documents and task boards.
The examination of code by other developers to find errors, security weaknesses and breaches of coding standards before it is accepted.
Agreed rules for writing code, such as naming conventions, layout, commenting and error handling, that make code consistent and maintainable.
Planned and systematic activities, such as reviews, inspections, testing and audits, that build quality into every stage of a project.
tips: When asked to 'explain what is meant by resources', give a definition and examples from different categories, such as a programmer (human), processing power (technical) and the budget (financial).
When you expand SMART, give a short explanation for each letter, not just the word. 'Agreed – signed off by both sides before development begins' earns the mark; 'Agreed' on its own may not.
If asked to describe a role, give two distinct responsibilities, ideally including what the person produces, such as 'the analyst produces the system specification'.
Link each feature to a benefit: 'CPA identifies tasks with float, so staff can be moved from them onto a delayed critical task, keeping the project on schedule.'

In graph questions, read the description slowly and label every version. Arrows always point from the older version to the newer one, and a rollback is shown by drawing the new version from the earlier node, not from the latest one.
This is a recall question with three marks available. Learn the three conditions as a set, using the textbook's ideas, then add a brief reason for each if the question says 'explain'.
When describing a CASE tool, always give a specific example and what it does, such as 'a debugger lets the programmer step through code and watch variable values'.

7.title: Security issues
terms: Malicious software, such as viruses, worms, Trojans, ransomware and spyware, written to damage or disrupt systems or to gain unauthorised access to data.
Malware that encrypts a victim's files and demands payment in exchange for the decryption key.
Malware that secretly records a user's activity, such as keystrokes, passwords or websites visited, and sends it to an attacker.
Malware disguised as legitimate software that the user installs; it carries a hidden harmful payload, such as a back door, and does not self-replicate.
Malware that attaches itself to a host file or program and spreads when the host is run or shared, so it needs user action to spread.
Standalone malware that replicates itself across a network without needing a host file or any user action, usually by exploiting unpatched vulnerabilities.
An attack in which many compromised devices (a botnet) flood a server or network with requests so that legitimate users cannot access it.
Gaining unauthorised access to a computer system or its data; an offence under the Computer Misuse Act 1990.
A social engineering attack using fraudulent emails, messages or websites that imitate trusted organisations to trick people into revealing personal details such as passwords.
Manipulating people into giving away confidential information or access, rather than attacking the technology directly.
The period during which a system is not operational and cannot be used.
A risk to data posed by people inside an organisation, such as employees or contractors, who misuse their legitimate access deliberately or carelessly.
Data that is needed for immediate, day-to-day use by an organisation.
Moving inactive data that is no longer needed for daily use from the live system to separate, secure long-term storage, indexed so that it can be retrieved later.
Data that is no longer needed for day-to-day operations but must be kept for reference, audit or legal reasons.
A copy of current data, taken regularly and stored separately from the original, so that data can be restored if it is lost or corrupted.
Using backed-up data to restore a system to a previously correct state after data has been lost or corrupted.
A record of the state of a system at the precise moment it was backed up, allowing the system to be returned to that state.
A record of every change made to a database since the last backup, which can be re-applied after a restore to bring the data up to date.
A formal document setting out the rules, procedures and responsibilities an organisation uses to protect its systems and data.
Permissions that determine which files, folders or records a user may access and what they may do with them, such as read-only or read and write.
The process of proving that a user is who they claim to be, using something they know, have or are.
Converting plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and a key so that it cannot be understood without the correct key.
Hardware or software that monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and blocks data that does not meet a set of security rules.
Authentication requiring two or more different types of evidence, such as a password (something you know) and a code sent to a phone (something you have).
A backup that copies every file altered since the most recent full backup, so it grows until the next full backup.
A backup that copies every file on the system, whether or not it has changed, each time it runs.
A backup that copies only files modified since the most recent backup of any kind, full or incremental.
A plan for keeping the whole organisation operating during and after a disruption, covering staff, premises and suppliers as well as IT.
The way an organisation recovers its IT systems and resumes operating after a catastrophic event, whether accidental, natural or deliberate.

A documented plan setting out how an organisation will restore its IT systems and data and resume operating after a catastrophic incident, identifying critical data, key personnel, backup and recovery processes and an alternative site.
In the CCEA textbook, the list of parts of the system that must be restored after a disaster; more widely, the maximum amount of data, measured in time, that can acceptably be lost.
The time limit within which each part of the system must be recovered after a disaster.
tips: Make the distinguishing feature explicit. 'A worm is a type of malware' earns nothing; 'a worm replicates itself across a network without needing a host file or any user action' earns the mark.

In consequences questions, apply each point to the organisation in the scenario. 'The clinic cannot see appointment lists, so patients are turned away' scores; 'the company loses money' alone often does not.
A definition worth full marks says the inactive data is moved to separate secure storage and can still be retrieved later, ideally through an index.

When asked about a restore point, say what it records (the state of the system at the moment of the backup), that the system is restored to that state, and that transactions made since can be re-applied.
When asked to describe the contents of a security policy, give a range of distinct items, each with a brief explanation, and link them to the threats in the scenario if there is one.

Recovery questions set in a context reward a clear sequence: name the full backup to restore, then the specific differential or each incremental by day, state the point in time the system is now at, then mention re-applying logged transactions. Practise restores regularly so staff know the procedure and the backups are proven to work.

Examiners usually credit the four contents (critical data, key personnel, backup and recovery processes, alternative site). Learn them as a set, and for 'suggest ways to meet the RTOs', link each technique to the scenario, e.g. off-site backups for a firm that keeps everything on one site.

8.title: Algorithms
terms: Software designed to carry out a particular task for the user, such as a word processor, spreadsheet or booking app.
A set of instructions that a computer executes in order to carry out a specific task.
A finite, ordered sequence of precise, unambiguous steps designed to solve a problem or complete a task.
The property that an algorithm must terminate after a limited number of steps.
Removing details that are not relevant to a problem so that only the essential features remain, giving a simpler model.
Breaking a complex problem down into smaller sub-problems that can be understood, solved and tested separately.
A top-down diagram showing a problem at the top broken into progressively smaller sub-problems below it.
A diagram that represents an algorithm using standard symbols (terminator, process, input/output, decision) joined by flow lines.
A programming construct in which a set of instructions is repeated, either a set number of times or until a condition is met.
A structured, language-independent, English-like way of describing an algorithm using keywords and indentation that resemble program code.
A construct in which a condition that evaluates to true or false determines which of two or more paths through the program is followed.
A special input value, such as -1, that signals the end of the data and stops a condition-controlled loop.
A programming construct in which instructions are carried out one after another in the order written.
Working through an algorithm or program by hand, step by step, to check its logic without using a computer.
An error in the design of an algorithm or program that causes incorrect results although the program still runs.
A table used during a dry run to record the value of each variable, any conditions and any output at each step of an algorithm.
A search of a sorted list that repeatedly compares the target with the middle item and discards the half that cannot contain it, until the item is found or no items remain.
Division that gives only the whole-number part of the result, discarding any remainder (/ on two integers in C#, DIV in pseudocode).
A search that checks each item in turn from the start of the list until the target is found or the end of the list is reached.
The input for which an algorithm does the least work, such as the target being the first item compared in a search.
A notation describing how the time or memory an algorithm needs grows as the size of its input grows, usually in the worst case and ignoring constant factors, e.g. O(n).
O(log n) growth, in which doubling the size of the input adds only a constant amount of extra work, as in binary search.
A measure of how the amount of memory an algorithm needs grows as the size of its input grows.
A measure of how the number of steps an algorithm takes grows as the size of its input grows.
The input for which an algorithm does the most work, such as the target being last or absent in a linear search.
A sort that repeatedly passes through a list comparing adjacent items and swapping them if they are in the wrong order, until a pass makes no swaps.
One complete traversal through a list (or the unsorted part of it) by a sorting algorithm.
A variable used to hold one value during a swap so that it is not overwritten and lost.
A sort that takes each item in turn and inserts it into its correct position within a growing sorted section of the list, shifting larger items along.
An approach that solves a problem by repeatedly breaking it into smaller sub-problems of the same type and combining their solutions.
Describes a sort that rearranges items within the original array, needing little or no extra memory.
A divide-and-conquer sort that splits a list repeatedly until each sub-list has one item, then merges the sub-lists back together in order.
The item chosen in quick sort around which the other items are partitioned into smaller and larger groups.
A divide-and-conquer sort that partitions a list around a pivot, with smaller items on one side and larger on the other, then sorts each partition in the same way.
A Boolean variable in a bubble sort that records whether any swap was made during a pass, so the sort can stop when a pass makes no swaps.
tips: For a one-mark 'describe the purpose of a program' question, the safest answer is: a set of instructions that the computer carries out to perform a specific task. Adding an example from the scenario never hurts.
Property questions usually give one mark for naming a property and one for explaining it. Tie each explanation to the scenario in the question – generic examples score less well.
In 'explain' questions, give the meaning and a benefit, and use the scenario: name actual sub-problems or actual details that would be left out.
Flowchart marks are lost for missing START/END terminators, using a rectangle for input or output, and decisions with only one labelled exit. Label every exit Yes/No.
In trace-table questions, follow the algorithm exactly as written – even if you can see it is wrong – and fill in every row. Marks are usually given per correct row or column.

Describe questions typically award a mark per step: sorted list; find middle; compare; stop if equal; discard the half that cannot contain the target; repeat until found or no items remain. Do not forget the 'not found' stopping condition.
If you write high = mid instead of mid - 1, a search for a missing value can loop forever. Examiners look for the ± 1.
When asked for a maximum number of comparisons, show the halving sequence or the power of 2 – method marks are available even if you slip on the final number.
Evaluate questions want two-sided points ('linear needs no sorting, whereas binary does') and a justified recommendation for the scenario in the question.
Examiners distinguish bubble and insertion traces by the intermediate lists. If a question asks for the list after pass 2 of an insertion sort, only the first three items will be in order.
A full merge sort description needs both halves: splitting down to single items and merging sorted sub-lists. A quick sort description needs the pivot, the partition and repeating on each side.

'Compare' and 'evaluate' answers are marked on developed, two-sided points. 'Merge sort is faster' earns little; 'merge sort is O(n log n) whereas bubble sort is O(n²), so for 50 000 records merge sort needs far fewer comparisons' earns full credit.

These are usually two-mark 'explain' questions: say what the feature does (the flag records whether any swap happened) and why it helps (the sort can stop early when no swaps occur, saving unnecessary passes).

9.title: Fundamentals of programming
terms: A software application that brings together the tools needed to develop programs, such as an editor, a translator and debugging tools, in one place.
A translator that converts assembly language into machine code, each mnemonic becoming one machine code instruction.
A translator that converts the whole of a high-level program into object code before it is executed, reporting all errors found.
A translator that translates and executes a high-level program one statement at a time, producing no object code.
Binary instructions that a particular processor can execute directly.
The translated (machine code) version of a program produced by a compiler or assembler, ready to be executed.
A program as written by the programmer in a programming language; readable by people but not directly executable by the processor.
Converting a program from the language in which it was written into machine code that the processor can execute.
A classification of data that determines the values a variable can hold, the memory it needs and the operations that can be performed on it.
The name given to a variable, constant or subroutine so that it can be referred to in a program.
The set of rules that define how valid statements must be written in a programming language.
A named location in memory that stores a single value which can change while the program is running.
A named value that is set when the program is written and cannot be changed while the program runs.
Converting a value from one data type to another, e.g. (double)total or (int)7.9.
An operator that gives the remainder after integer division (% in C#, MOD in pseudocode).
A loop that repeats while or until a condition is met, so the number of repetitions need not be known in advance.
A loop that repeats a number of times known before it starts, such as a for loop.
An if statement placed inside another if or else block, so the inner decision is only made when the outer condition has a particular result.
A loop whose terminating condition is never met, usually because nothing in the body changes the condition.
A loop that tests its condition after each pass, so the body always runs at least once (do…while, REPEAT…UNTIL).
A loop that tests its condition before each pass, so the body may run zero times (while).
A loop placed inside the body of another loop; the inner loop runs completely for each pass of the outer loop.
A subroutine that performs a task and returns a single value to the point where it was called.
A prewritten, tested subroutine supplied with a language or obtained from elsewhere that can be called in a program.
A subroutine that performs a task but does not return a value (return type void in C#).
A named, self-contained block of code that performs a specific task and can be called from elsewhere in a program.
A value supplied to a method when it is called, matching one of its parameters in order and type.
A variable named in a subroutine's header that receives a value (the argument) when the subroutine is called.
Passing a reference to (the address of) a variable, so changes made to the parameter in the subroutine change the original variable.
Passing a copy of an argument's value to a subroutine, so changes made to the parameter do not affect the original variable.
A variable that can be accessed from any part of the program and exists for the whole run.
A variable declared inside a subroutine or block that can only be accessed there and exists only while it runs.
The region of a program in which a variable can be accessed.
Dividing a program into separate, self-contained modules (subroutines), each performing one clearly defined task.
A data structure whose size can grow or shrink while the program is running, such as a list.
A data structure whose size is fixed when it is created and cannot change while the program runs, such as an array.
A static data structure that holds a fixed number of elements of the same data type under one identifier, each accessed by an index.
The position number used to access an element of an array or list; in C# the first index is 0.
An array whose elements are arranged in rows and columns and accessed using two indexes, [row, column].
A dynamic data structure holding items of one type whose size changes at run time as items are added or removed.
One named item of data within a record, such as a member's name or age.
A data structure that groups a fixed set of related, named fields, which may be of different data types, to describe one item.
A character, such as a comma, used to separate the fields of a record stored on one line of a text file.
A file of characters, usually organised in lines, stored on secondary storage so that data persists between program runs.
Storage that keeps data after the program ends or power is removed, such as a file on secondary storage.
A program that copes with invalid input and unexpected events without crashing or producing incorrect results.
An object created when a run-time error occurs, which stops the program unless it is handled, for example in a try…catch structure.
An error that occurs while the program is running when an impossible operation is attempted, such as division by zero, often causing a crash.
A statement that follows the syntax rules but has no valid meaning, such as assigning text to an integer variable.
An error that breaks the grammatical rules of the programming language, so the program cannot be compiled or run.
Valid test data at the boundaries of the allowed range, or at a point where processing changes, such as the highest and lowest values accepted.
A marker set in the IDE that pauses execution at a chosen line so the program's state can be examined.
A debugger display of the chain of subroutine calls that led to the current line of execution.
Executing a program one line at a time in the IDE, either entering called subroutines (step into) or running them as one step (step over).
tips: 'Describe three features of an IDE' is usually marked as feature + how it helps, so 'syntax highlighting (1) colours keywords so the structure of the code is easier to read (1)'. A bare list of names rarely earns more than one mark per pair.
Comparison questions are marked in matched pairs. Write both sides of each difference, e.g. 'a compiler produces an executable file, whereas an interpreter produces no object code'.
When asked to suggest a data type, give a reason tied to the data: 'string, because the mobile number begins with 0 and is not used in calculations'. A type with no reason may not get the mark.

A two-mark 'why use a constant?' answer needs the reason and its effect: 'its value cannot be changed accidentally while the program runs (1) and if the rate changes it only needs to be edited in one place (1)'.
In evaluation questions, show each stage: substituted values, then true/false for each comparison, then the final result. Working often earns marks even if the final answer slips.

In code-writing answers, credit is commonly given for a prompt, the input, the correct conversion and well-labelled output. Prompts like "Enter the number of nights: " show the examiner you have thought about the user.

In 'explain with reference to the algorithm' questions, one mark is usually for the definition and one for pointing to where it occurs. Quote the line: 'the IF total > 100 statement applies the discount only when the condition is true'.
When writing a chain for bands, test boundaries with the edge values. For 'Silver is 75 to 89', check that 74, 75, 89 and 90 all give the right award.
When asked how many times a loop runs, list the counter values rather than guessing. It takes seconds and removes off-by-one slips.
'Compare while and do…while' needs where the condition is tested and the consequence: 'a while loop may not execute at all, whereas a do…while always executes at least once'.
In trace questions write every value in order; examiners award marks row by row, and a correct final answer with no working may score less than a full, careful trace.
The single distinguishing point for the mark is 'a function returns a value to the calling code; a procedure does not'. State it explicitly.
Check headers carefully in code questions: return type, name, parameter types and order. Marks are often given separately for a correct header and a correct return.
A full answer states what is passed (copy versus reference/address) and the consequence for the original variable (protected versus changed). Each half typically earns a mark.
Advantage questions want specific, linked points: 'local variables can only be changed within their own subroutine, so a bug affecting one is easier to locate'. Avoid vague 'it is easier'.
Write each benefit as a two-part point, feature then consequence: 'each module can be tested independently (1), so errors are easier to locate (1)'.

Static/dynamic questions need both sides plus an example: 'an array is static because its size is fixed when it is created, whereas a list is dynamic because items can be added or removed while the program runs'.
Code questions usually award marks for the declaration, a loop with correct bounds (start at 0, < Length), correct indexing and correct output. Write the bounds carefully.
'List, because the number of bookings changes during the day' earns the mark; 'list, because it is better' does not. Always give the property and the link to the scenario.
The key words for a record definition are 'related fields' and 'different data types'. Contrast with an array, where every element has the same type.
File-handling code typically earns marks for: opening in the correct mode, a loop that reads/writes one line at a time, splitting on the delimiter, converting types and closing the file.
'Why are files needed?' wants the contrast: 'data in variables is held in RAM and lost when the program ends (1); a file on secondary storage keeps it so it can be reloaded next time (1)'.
Name the check and link it to the field in the scenario: 'a range check that the number of nights is between 1 and 14'. A generic list of checks earns very little.
When asked how a program could handle invalid input robustly, mention both: validation loops to reject bad input, and try…catch so that unexpected run-time errors give a message rather than a crash.
Classify an error by its effect and give a specific example: 'a logic error, because the program runs but outputs the wrong price for a 65-year-old'.
Give actual values, their category and the expected outcome: '65, boundary, should be charged £2.50'. 'Test with a boundary value' alone will not score.

A debugging-tool answer needs what the tool does and how it helps locate the error, e.g. 'a breakpoint pauses execution at a chosen line (1) so the values of variables at that point can be inspected to see whether they are as expected (1)'.
Write matched pairs: 'a compiler reports all syntax errors before the program runs, whereas an interpreter only reports one when it reaches that line'.

10.title: Object-oriented programming
terms: A data item declared in a class; each object holds its own value for it, and together these values form the object's state.
A template or blueprint that defines the attributes and methods (behaviours) shared by all objects of one type.
A special method with the same name as the class and no return type that runs automatically when an object is created, to initialise its attributes.
Creating a new object from a class; in C# this is done with the new keyword, which calls the constructor.
A subroutine defined in a class that describes an action an object can perform or that can be performed on it.
A specific instance of a class, holding its own values for the attributes the class defines.
The part of a method header, in brackets, stating the data items (each with a type and name) the method must be given when it is called.
The data type of the value a method sends back to the code that called it; void if it returns nothing.
Combining data and the methods that act on it in a class, and hiding the data (private) so that it can only be accessed or changed through the class's methods.
A public method that returns the current value of a private attribute.
A class member with get and/or set blocks that gives controlled access to a private field using attribute-style syntax.
A public method that takes a new value as a parameter and uses it to change a private attribute, often after validating it.
A UML diagram showing a class as a box with three compartments – name, attributes and methods – using +, - and # for public, private and protected.
An access modifier making a member visible inside its own class and any subclasses but hidden from all other code; shown as # in a class diagram.
A general class whose attributes and methods are inherited by one or more more specialised classes.
The tree-like structure of classes related by inheritance, with the most general class at the top and subclasses below it.
A more specialised class that inherits the attributes and methods of a base class and usually adds its own.
The mechanism by which a new, more specialised class (subclass) takes on the attributes and methods of an existing, more general class (superclass) and can add its own or modify inherited ones.
A class that cannot be instantiated; objects must be created from its subclasses, which must override any abstract methods it declares.
Defining several methods in the same class with the same name but different parameter lists; the compiler chooses one from the arguments given.
Redefining an inherited method in a subclass with the same name, parameters and return type, so the subclass's version runs for its objects.
The ability of objects of different classes to respond to the same method call in different ways, usually through overriding.
An object on a graphical user interface, such as a button or text box, that has properties, methods and events.
An action or occurrence that a program can detect and respond to, such as a mouse click, key press or timer tick.
A subroutine that runs automatically when a particular event occurs on a particular control.
A programming paradigm in which the flow of the program is determined by events, such as user actions, sensor outputs or messages.
tips: When a question says 'by referring to the code', name the actual identifiers: e.g. 'LibraryBook is the class; b1 and b2 are objects; title is an attribute; Lend() is a method'. A general definition on its own gets only part of the marks.
A setter normally has one parameter and a void return type; a getter normally has an empty parameter list and returns the attribute's type. Examiners check for exactly this pattern.
A full-mark definition has three parts: data and methods combined in a class; attributes made private; accessed or changed only through get/set methods. Add a benefit if the question says 'explain'.
In output questions, look for conditions inside methods that silently refuse a change – they are where most marks are lost.
If asked to draw a class diagram from code, copy the identifiers exactly and give every attribute and parameter its data type – these are the usual marking points.
A complete definition needs both halves: the subclass inherits the attributes and methods of the superclass, and it can add its own or change inherited ones.

Exam answers that write a subclass are marked on: the colon and base class name; new private attributes; a constructor that calls base(...) with the right arguments; assignment of the new attributes; and any extra or overriding methods.
Support a polymorphism definition with an example from the question: name the method that is overridden and say what each class does differently.

'Evaluate' questions are levels-marked and often worth 6 or more marks. One-word lists ('reusable, complex') reach only the lowest level. Develop each point with why, cover both sides, and end with a judgement.
Use the three terms precisely – event, event handler, control – and describe the sequence: event occurs on a control → handler runs → output/properties updated.

1.title: Data representation
terms: The base-2 number system, which uses only the digits 0 and 1; column values are powers of 2.
A binary digit; the smallest unit of data, which stores either 0 or 1.
A group of 8 bits, which can represent 256 (2⁸) different values, such as one character.
A group of 4 bits; half a byte, represented by one hexadecimal digit.
A whole number stored with no sign bit, so every bit represents magnitude and only zero or positive values (0 to 2ⁿ − 1) are possible.
The base-10 number system, using the digits 0–9 with column values that are powers of 10.
The rightmost bit of a binary number, with a place value of 1.
The leftmost bit of a binary number, which has the highest place value.
The value of a column in a number, determined by its position and the base, e.g. 128, 64, 32 … 1 in an 8-bit binary number.
A base-16 number system using the digits 0–9 and A–F, in which each digit represents exactly one nibble (4 bits).
A representation in which each denary digit is stored separately as its own 4-bit binary code (0000–1001).
Adding binary numbers column by column from the right using the rules 0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+1=0 carry 1 and 1+1+1=1 carry 1.
A bit passed to the next column on the left when a column total is two or more.
The smallest and largest values a representation can store with a given number of bits, e.g. −128 to +127 in 8-bit two's complement.
A signed-integer representation in which the MSB shows the sign (0 positive, 1 negative) and the remaining bits give the size of the number.
The most significant bit of a signed number, used to show whether the value is positive or negative.
A signed-integer representation in which the MSB has a negative place value (−128 in 8 bits); a number is negated by inverting its bits and adding 1.
An error that occurs when the result of a calculation is too large (or too far negative) to be represented in the available number of bits.
A bit in the processor's status register that is set when a signed arithmetic operation overflows.
The point separating the whole-number bits from the fractional bits, whose place values are ½, ¼, ⅛ and so on.
A way of storing real numbers in which the binary point is at an agreed position that does not change, so a set number of bits holds the fraction.
A number that can have a fractional part, such as 6.75 or −0.3125.
The part of a floating-point number that states how many places, and in which direction, the binary point is moved.
A way of storing real numbers as a mantissa multiplied by 2 raised to an exponent, so the binary point can move and a wide range of values can be held.
The part of a floating-point number that holds its significant bits; in this course a two's complement fraction with the point after the sign bit.
Adjusting a floating-point number so the first two bits of the mantissa differ (0.1 or 1.0), maximising precision and giving each value a unique representation.
How finely values can be distinguished, determined by the number of significant (mantissa) bits.
The span between the largest and smallest magnitudes that can be represented, determined mainly by the number of exponent bits.
The difference between a real value and the nearest value that can be stored in the available bits.
An error that occurs when a value is too close to zero to be represented with the available exponent, so it is stored as zero or loses precision.
An agreed list of characters that a computer system can represent, in which each character is given a unique binary code.
A non-printing character code, such as carriage return, line feed or tab, used to control how text is processed or displayed.
American Standard Code for Information Interchange: a 7-bit character set of 128 codes covering English letters, digits, punctuation and control characters.
An 8-bit extension of ASCII giving 256 codes; codes 0–127 match ASCII and codes 128–255 hold accented letters and symbols, which vary between code pages.
A character standard that gives a unique code point to characters from almost all of the world's writing systems, plus symbols and emoji; its first 128 codes match ASCII.
A variable-length Unicode encoding that uses one byte for ASCII characters and two to four bytes for other characters.
An extra bit added to a group of bits so that the total number of 1s is even (even parity) or odd (odd parity), allowing transmission errors to be detected.
An extra digit calculated from the other digits of a code number and added to the end, so the computer can detect entry or reading errors by recalculating it.

A check digit method in which each digit is multiplied by a weighting, the products are added, and the check digit is found from the remainder after dividing by 11 (0 gives 0, 1 gives X, otherwise 11 minus the remainder).
An input error in which two characters are entered in the wrong order, such as 47019 instead of 40719.
An image stored as a grid of pixels, with the colour of each pixel held as a binary number.
The number of bits used to represent the colour of each pixel; n bits give 2ⁿ possible colours, and more bits give a larger file.
Short for picture element: the smallest addressable element of a bitmap image, storing a single colour as a binary value.
The blocky appearance of a bitmap image when it is enlarged beyond its resolution so that individual pixels become visible.
The number of pixels in an image, usually given as width × height in pixels, or as dots per inch (dpi) for printed images.
A colour model in which each colour is made by mixing red, green and blue light; 24-bit RGB stores one byte (0–255) for each component.
Exchangeable Image File Format metadata added by cameras and phones, such as date and time, camera model, exposure settings and GPS location.
Data about data, such as an image's width, height and colour depth, stored with the file so that software can interpret it correctly.
An image stored as a set of objects described by mathematical properties such as coordinates, size and colour, so it can be scaled without loss of quality.
A device that measures an analogue signal at regular intervals and converts each measurement into a binary value.
The principle that the sampling rate must be at least twice the highest frequency in the signal for it to be reproduced accurately.
The number of bits used to store each sound sample, which determines how precisely each amplitude is recorded.
The number of samples of an analogue sound wave taken per second, measured in hertz.
tips: A definition such as 'a kilobyte is 1024 bytes' or '2¹⁰ bytes' earns the mark; 'about 1000 bytes' on its own may not. In calculations, show each ×1024 or ÷1024 step and give the unit with the final answer.

Conversions usually carry one mark for working and one for the answer. Show the place-value row, the subtractions or the remainders, then check by converting back. Reading remainders top-down (giving the bits reversed) is the most common slip.

Examiners want the idea that each digit is coded separately in four bits, plus a named use such as a digital clock. For 'compare' questions, contrast BCD with pure binary on storage, display and arithmetic.
Show the carry row clearly – it is often where the method mark is. Then convert the result to denary to prove it is correct, and state whether overflow has occurred if the question asks.

'Explain a limitation' questions want a specific consequence, e.g. 'there are two zeros, so one bit pattern is wasted and comparisons with zero need two checks', or a worked sum showing a wrong result.
Forgetting to add 1 is the most common error, giving an answer that is one too small in magnitude. Converting back is the quickest way to catch it.

In a subtraction question, say explicitly 'add the two's complement of 23' and 'the carry out of the most significant bit is discarded'. Showing −B in binary and the carry row usually secures the method marks.
When asked whether overflow has occurred, answer yes/no and justify with numbers: 'the true answer is 150, which is greater than 127, the largest value in 8-bit two's complement'.
Always show the place-value row including the fractional columns. When converting denary to fixed point, write the value as a sum of powers of two first, e.g. 9.375 = 8 + 1 + 0.25 + 0.125.
Floating-point decoding is marked step by step: write the exponent in denary, show the mantissa with the point moved, then the place-value sum. A correct method with one slip still earns most marks.

'Explain why floating-point numbers are normalised' needs both ideas – maximum precision from the mantissa bits and a single unique representation of each value. In a normalising question give both the new mantissa and the new exponent in binary.

For 'explain the effect of changing the split' questions, give the direction of change for both range and precision, with a reason: 'more exponent bits increase the range because the point can move further, but precision falls because there are fewer mantissa bits'.
A two-mark definition needs both halves: the list of characters a system can represent and a unique binary code for each. For 'why a standard', link it to exchanging text between different computers.

When comparing, quote the numbers (128, 256, over a million) and give a consequence: 'Unicode can represent many more languages, but each non-English character may take two to four bytes, so files are larger and slower to transmit'.

For a parity calculation, state the parity type, count the 1s explicitly, give the parity bit and the complete byte. Limitations must be specific: 'two flipped bits leave the parity unchanged', not 'parity is unreliable'.
'Explain the effect' answers need a chain: 'a greater colour depth means more bits per pixel, so more colours and smoother shading, but every pixel needs more bits, so the file is larger'.
Name specific items (width, height, colour depth) and say why each is needed. 'It stores information about the image' alone is too vague for credit.
Use paired comparison points (stored as…, when scaled…, file size depends on…, suited to…) and apply them to the scenario. 'Vectors are better quality' without a reason earns little.

'Describe how sound is digitised' needs the sequence: the analogue signal is sampled at regular intervals, the amplitude of each sample is measured, and it is stored as a binary number with a fixed number of bits.

2.title: Data and information
terms: The surrounding detail – what a value measures, about whom, when and in what units – that gives data its meaning.
Raw facts and figures, such as numbers, text, dates, images or sound, that have no context and therefore no meaning on their own.
Data that has been processed and given context so that it has meaning to the person using it.
The result of applying one or more rules to information so that an informed decision can be made.
The extent to which information is up to date, reflecting the situation now rather than when the data was collected.
Garbage in, garbage out: if the input data is of poor quality, the output information will also be of poor quality, however good the system.
The extent to which information comes from a trustworthy, authoritative source and has been verified, so that it can be depended on.
An input error in which data is copied or typed incorrectly, such as 2500 entered instead of 250.
The accuracy, consistency and completeness of data throughout its life, protected by measures such as validation and verification.
A validation check that data matches a set pattern of characters, such as two letters followed by four digits.
A validation check that the correct number of characters has been entered, or that the entry is within a minimum and maximum length.
A validation check that compares the entered value with a list or file of valid values.
A validation check that a field has not been left blank.
A validation check that a value lies between a lower and an upper limit, e.g. >= 1 AND <= 15.
A validation check that data is of the correct data type, such as an integer rather than text.
An automatic check that input data is sensible and in the expected form, such as a presence, range, length, type or format check; it cannot prove the data is correct.
In a check digit calculation, the multiplier given to each digit according to its position; in Modulus 11 it starts at 2 for the rightmost digit and rises by 1 to the left.
A validation check in which the number of documents in a batch is counted by hand and compared with the number entered by the computer.
A total of a meaningful field on every document in a batch, such as total hours worked, compared with the computer's total to check all documents were entered once.
A total of a field whose sum has no meaning, such as ID numbers, compared with the computer's total to check all documents in a batch were entered exactly once.
A verification method in which data is entered twice and the computer compares the two versions, flagging any difference.
A verification method in which entered data is compared by eye with the source document, ideally by a different person.
A check that data has been entered or copied accurately, so that it exactly matches the original source.
The process of getting data into a computer system, either manually (e.g. keying from forms) or automatically (e.g. barcodes, OMR, sensors).
Software that recognises printed or written characters in a scanned image and converts them into editable text.
An automated data capture method in which a scanner detects marks made in set positions on a form, such as a multiple-choice answer sheet.
Processing in which transactions are collected over a period in a transaction file and processed together as one job at a later time, without user interaction.
The main, relatively permanent file of records in a system, such as all customers' accounts, which transactions update.
Real-time processing of sensor input within a guaranteed, very short time so that the output can affect the next input, e.g. anti-lock brakes.
Processing in which each transaction or input is dealt with as soon as it occurs, so the master file is always up to date.
Real-time processing in which each transaction is processed as it occurs while the user waits, so the master file is always up to date, e.g. bookings and cash machines.
Preventing other users from changing a record while one user is updating it, to avoid lost updates and double-booking in multi-user systems.
A file holding the transactions (changes) collected over a period, used to update a master file.
A system that allows many users to share the same computer's resources at the same time, each with their own session and permissions.
The apparent running of several programs at once by rapidly switching the processor between them in time slices.
Running several threads, each a separate path of execution, within one program so that they run concurrently and share its memory.
tips: For 'distinguish' questions mark schemes typically give a mark per level: definition plus a correct example from the scenario. A knowledge answer that does not state the rule being applied usually does not get the mark.

A typical 2-mark answer names the factor (1) and explains its effect in context (1): ‘Incomplete – the re-order message does not say which pack size to buy, so the wrong stock may be ordered.’ Simply listing the six factors earns little beyond a 'state' question.

Mark schemes credit a precise rule: ‘range check: hour >= 0 AND <= 23’ beats ‘check the hour is sensible’. Never write that validation checks data is 'correct' or 'accurate' – say 'sensible', 'reasonable' or 'within acceptable limits'.
