Calculation questions are usually 3–4 marks: one for correct weightings/products, one for the checksum, one for the remainder, one for the check digit. To 'show a number is invalid', recalculate including the check digit at weighting 1 and state that the remainder is not 0.

In 'demonstrate' questions, name a specific field from the documents for each total and say what is compared with what. Explaining why a hash total catches an error that a batch total misses usually earns an extra mark.
For 'describe a verification method' give how it works (1) plus a feature or drawback (1). Do not call double entry a validation check – it is verification.
'Explain two limitations' (4 marks): state the limitation (1) and illustrate it with an example or consequence (1), once for validation and once for verification.
When recommending a method, link it to the scenario: 'OMR suits a 2 000-pupil multiple-choice test because answers are marks in fixed positions, so sheets can be read quickly and accurately.'

In 'select and justify' questions, name the method and link it to a feature of the application, e.g. 'real-time transaction processing, because the seat must be removed from sale immediately to prevent double-booking'.

3.title: Architecture
terms: The processor: the component, made up of the control unit, ALU and registers, that fetches, decodes and executes program instructions to process data.
A circuit in the processor that generates a regular stream of electrical pulses used to synchronise and time all of the processor's operations.
The main printed circuit board of a computer, holding the processor socket, memory slots, expansion slots, I/O controllers and ports; its tracks form the buses.
The part of the CPU that carries out arithmetic operations (such as addition) and logical operations (such as AND, OR and comparisons) on values held in registers.
The part of the CPU that manages the fetch–decode–execute cycle, sends control signals to coordinate and monitor the hardware, and controls the input and output of data.
A single, very fast storage location inside the CPU that temporarily holds the data, instruction or address currently being processed.
A special-purpose register that holds the results of arithmetic and logic operations carried out by the ALU.
A special-purpose register that holds the instruction currently being decoded and executed.
A special-purpose register that holds the address of the memory location about to be read from or written to; its contents are placed on the address bus.
A special-purpose register that holds data or an instruction just read from memory, or data waiting to be written to memory; a two-way buffer between CPU and memory.
A special-purpose register that holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched; it is incremented during each fetch.
The unidirectional part of the system bus that carries the address of the memory location or I/O device to be accessed, from the CPU outwards.
The number of parallel lines in a bus, and so the number of bits it can carry at the same time.
The bidirectional part of the system bus that carries command and timing signals such as memory read, memory write, clock and interrupt requests.
The bidirectional part of the system bus that carries data and instructions between the CPU, main memory and I/O devices.
The set of parallel connections – address, data and control buses – that links the processor, main memory and I/O controllers.
The largest amount of memory a processor can access: 2^(address bus width) locations, each holding as many bits as the data bus width.
An electronic circuit between the system bus and a peripheral that performs protocol, voltage and data-format conversion and buffers data between devices of different speeds.
A device outside the processor, main memory and system bus that provides input, output or storage, such as a keyboard, printer or external drive.
The physical connection point on a computer where a peripheral's cable is plugged in, through which data passes to and from the I/O controller.
Universal Serial Bus: a standard defining the cables, connectors and protocols used to connect peripherals, carrying both data and power.
A computer design in which program instructions and data are stored together in the same main memory and a single processor fetches and executes them in sequence over a shared bus.
The limit on performance caused by instructions and data sharing one memory and bus, so they cannot be fetched at the same time and the processor waits for memory.
The continuous process by which the CPU fetches an instruction from main memory, decodes it into opcode and operand, and carries it out, then repeats for the next instruction.
The complete set of machine-code instructions that a particular processor (or processor family) is designed to recognise and execute.
The part of a machine-code instruction that specifies the operation to be performed, such as LOAD, ADD or JUMP.
The part of a machine-code instruction that holds the data to be used or the address where that data is stored.
Overlapping the fetch, decode and execute stages of successive instructions so that a new instruction is fetched while earlier ones are being decoded and executed, increasing throughput.
The number of clock cycles a processor carries out per second, measured in hertz (e.g. 3.2 GHz = 3.2 × 10⁹ cycles per second).
An independent processing unit within a CPU, with its own control unit, ALU and registers, able to fetch, decode and execute its own instructions.
A single processor chip containing two or more independent cores that can execute instructions at the same time.
A sequence of instructions within a program that can be scheduled to run independently, for example on a separate core.
The number of bits a processor can handle as a single unit in one operation, usually equal to the width of its general registers (e.g. 64-bit).
A standard set of tasks run on different computers so that their performance can be timed and compared fairly.
Floating-point operations per second: a measure of how quickly a processor performs arithmetic on real numbers.
Millions of instructions per second: a measure of how quickly a processor executes general instructions.
The memory the processor can address directly, made up of RAM and ROM, holding the programs and data currently in use.
Describes memory or storage that keeps its contents when the power is switched off, such as ROM, flash memory and hard disks.
Random access memory: volatile, read/write main memory that holds the operating system, programs and data currently in use.
Read-only memory: non-volatile main memory whose contents are fixed when made, used for start-up firmware and the programs of embedded systems.
Describes memory that loses its contents when the power is switched off, such as RAM.
The device that transfers data from RAM into cache, predicting and pre-fetching the data the processor is likely to need next.
Small, very fast and expensive memory on or beside the processor that holds frequently used instructions and data and data read ahead from RAM, reducing slower RAM accesses.
A severe loss of performance when the computer spends more time swapping pages between RAM and virtual memory than processing.
A fixed-size block of memory used by the operating system when moving data between RAM and virtual memory.
An area of secondary storage used by the operating system as an extension of RAM when RAM is full, with pages swapped between them as needed.
Non-volatile storage that keeps programs and data permanently when the power is off, such as a hard disk, SSD, optical disc or tape.
Data can be read from any location without reading the data before it, as on a hard disk, SSD or optical disc.
A magnetic storage device with spinning platters divided into tracks and sectors, read and written by heads on a moving arm, giving direct access.
Storage in which a laser writes and reads marks on the reflective layer of a spinning disc, such as a CD, DVD or Blu-ray disc.
A section of a track on a disk; the smallest area that is read or written as a unit.
Data must be read in order from the start until the required item is reached, as on magnetic tape.
One of the concentric circles into which the surface of a disk is divided for storing data.
A flash-memory drive fitted inside a computer in place of a hard disk, giving faster access, lower power use and greater robustness.
Non-volatile storage using flash memory, which holds data as electrical charges in semiconductor cells with no moving parts, e.g. SSDs, USB sticks and memory cards.
The simultaneous use of two or more processors or cores to work on different parts of the same task.
A computer system built into a larger device to perform one dedicated function, such as a heating controller or a car's braking system.
A computer design with physically separate memories and buses for instructions and for data, so an instruction and data can be accessed at the same time.
Complex instruction set computer: a processor with a large set of variable-length instructions, some of which carry out several low-level operations and take several clock cycles.
Reduced instruction set computer: a processor with a small set of simple, fixed-length instructions, most executed in one clock cycle, with only load and store accessing memory.
An additional processor that takes over a specific type of work from the main CPU, such as graphics, image processing or AI calculations.
A processor with many simple cores designed to perform the same operation on many data items in parallel, used for graphics and other highly parallel tasks.
Single instruction, multiple data: a form of parallel processing in which one instruction is applied to many data items at the same time.
tips: A 'describe the internal components' question wants a purpose for each component, not just its name. 'Clock – sends regular pulses that synchronise the processor's operations' earns the mark; 'clock – tells the time' does not.

'What three tasks does the control unit perform?' is a classic 3-mark question. Give three different tasks: running the cycle, coordinating/monitoring hardware with control signals, and controlling input and output of data.
For 'describe the purpose', give what it holds plus one detail: 'The PC holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched (1) and is incremented after each fetch (1).'
A 'describe the function of the three buses' answer gets one mark per bus for what it carries; add the direction with a reason to secure any extra marks.
Show each line of working in powers of two. Method marks are awarded even if the final figure slips; a bare answer that is wrong scores nothing.
Examiners credit reasons tied to differences between devices: 'devices operate at different speeds, so the controller buffers data' earns two marks; 'to connect the device' earns none.

A 6-mark description should cover shared memory, the stored-program idea, sequential fetch–execute, the three buses, I/O and secondary storage, and the bottleneck. Missing the limitation caps the mark.
One mark per correct, correctly ordered step. Name each register in full the first time and say what moves where: 'the contents of the PC are copied to the MAR'.

If asked for a pipelining diagram, draw time units (T1, T2…) down the side and instructions across, stagger each instruction by one unit, label F, D, E, and state the total. Unlabelled boxes lose the marks.

'Evaluate' needs both sides: say how the factor improves speed and when it does not. 'More cores let several threads execute at once, but a single-threaded program would see no benefit' scores far better than 'more cores is faster'.
Link each factor to its mechanism: 'more RAM means less data has to be swapped to slower secondary storage' rather than 'more RAM makes it faster'.
For 'why is clock speed not a good measure', give a reason: 'processors with different architectures complete different amounts of work per clock cycle'.

In 'which would you recommend' questions, the recommendation alone earns little. The marks are for linking each feature to the scenario: 'video editing software is multi-threaded, so the four cores of B can render in parallel'.
A 'difference between RAM and ROM' answer must make the contrast explicit: 'RAM is volatile whereas ROM is non-volatile'. Two separate lists of facts score less.
A 'using a diagram, explain how a computer uses cache' answer should show the CPU, cache, cache controller and RAM, label the check-cache, hit and miss paths, and mention reading ahead.
Describe virtual memory as a process: RAM full → pages moved to secondary storage → swapped back when needed → slower performance. That sequence is what earns the marks.

'List three benefits' and 'list three factors' are different questions – benefits are capacity, portability and security; factors are speed, capacity, durability, portability, reliability and cost. Read which one is asked.
'Fast' alone earns little. 'An SSD has faster access than a hard disk because it has no moving parts' earns the mark.
Questions often say 'do not use the same device or reason twice'. Plan all parts before you start writing so you do not run out of different devices or reasons.
For 'describe parallel processing', include all three ideas: two or more processors/cores, working at the same time, on different parts of the same task.
Comparison marks come from paired points: 'In Von Neumann instructions and data share one bus, whereas Harvard has separate buses so both can be fetched at once.'
Avoid absolute claims such as 'RISC is always faster'. Link each feature to a consequence: fewer transistors → less power → longer battery life.

When asked why a GPU suits a task, mention many simple cores and the same operation applied to many data items in parallel, then link to the task: 'each pixel of a frame needs the same shading calculation'.
In extended questions, apply every point to the scenario and finish with a justified recommendation. A list of facts about architectures with no link to the scenario sits in the lowest band.

4.title: User interface and data compression
terms: The study and design of how people interact with computers, aiming to make systems effective, efficient and satisfying to use.
The means by which a user and a computer communicate, including what is displayed or heard and how the user gives input.
A user interface in which the user types commands in an exact syntax at a prompt for the computer to carry out.
A user interface that guides the user through a structured on-screen form using text boxes, drop-down lists, check boxes and radio buttons.
A user interface that uses windows, icons, menus and a pointer (WIMP) to allow the user to interact visually.
An extra parameter typed after a command in a command line interface to modify what the command does, e.g. /s.
Software that converts spoken words, captured by a microphone, into text or commands.
A user interface operated by measuring a physical characteristic of the user, such as a fingerprint, face or iris.
A user interface that presents the user with a limited list of options to choose from, often arranged in levels.
A user interface that accepts requests typed or spoken in ordinary everyday language.
A user interface operated by finger gestures, such as tapping, swiping and pinching, on a touch screen.
A user interface that is controlled by spoken commands, using speech recognition.
Designing systems so they can be used by people with a wide range of abilities, including visual, hearing, motor and cognitive impairments.
Assistive software that reads the text and alternative text on screen aloud, or outputs it to a braille display, for users with visual impairments.
The original file size divided by the compressed file size, e.g. 12 MB → 3 MB is 4 : 1.
Encoding data using fewer bits than the original representation, to reduce storage space and transmission time.
Repeated or predictable data in a file that can be stored more efficiently, which is what compression removes.
An uncompressed image format that stores the colour of every pixel in a grid as a binary number.
Compression that reduces file size without losing any data, so the original can be reconstructed exactly.
Compression that permanently removes data judged less important, giving smaller files that cannot be restored exactly.
A lossless compression method that stores repeated patterns once in a dictionary and replaces each occurrence with a short reference (token).
A lossless compression method that replaces each run of identical values with a count and a single copy of the value.
A lossless method of compressing one or more files into a single archive file with a .zip extension.
A file (.txt) containing only characters, with no formatting, that can be opened by almost any program on any platform.
Waveform Audio File Format: an audio format that normally stores sound as uncompressed samples, giving high quality but large files.
Graphics Interchange Format: an image format using up to 256 colours from a palette chosen for the image, compressed losslessly; supports animation.
Joint Photographic Experts Group format: an image format that applies adjustable lossy compression to 24-bit colour images, suited to photographs.
Moving Picture Experts Group: a family of standards for storing compressed video and audio using lossy compression; MPEG-4 is usually stored as .mp4.
tips: A 'state four features' question earns one mark each for named features; 'describe' needs the feature plus what it means or an example. 'Easy to use' on its own is too vague – say why it is easy, e.g. consistent layout so learning transfers.
If asked what WIMP stands for, give all four words; 'mouse' is not the M, and 'pointer' is the P. 'Windows' means screen windows, not the Microsoft product.

'Why might an advanced programmer prefer a command line?' – link speed to knowing the commands, and mention scripting or low resource use. Extended evaluation questions need advantages and disadvantages for the named users before a recommendation.

'Describe how a smartphone user could input text, sound and video' (3 marks) – one specific method for each: e.g. on-screen keyboard with predictive text; voice note via built-in microphone; rear camera recording video.

For 'describe two disadvantages of voice interfaces' (4 marks), give each disadvantage and its consequence: 'background noise interferes with recognition (1), so commands are misheard and must be repeated (1)'.
In accessibility questions, name the feature and the user it helps: 'captions on videos (1) so users with hearing impairments can follow the content (1)'.

Mark schemes for 'two reasons for compression' credit exactly these two: to reduce file size and so storage space (1), and to reduce transmission (upload/download) time (1). 'Makes the file smaller' alone counts only once.
Show every stage – pixels, bytes per pixel, total, unit conversion – and label the units. A correct method with an arithmetic slip still earns most marks; a bare answer earns at most one.
'What difference would lossless compression have made?' – no loss of quality (1) but a larger file / less reduction in size (1). Always state that lossy loss is permanent.
In application questions count characters carefully: the encoded RLE string includes the digits of every count. Common error: calling RLE or GIF lossy – both are lossless.
'Why zip rather than use lossy compression?' – zipping is lossless so there is no loss of quality (1); the original is restored exactly when unzipped (1).

'Evaluate' needs a strength and a weakness for the stated purpose – e.g. 'WAV is suitable for the podcast's master recording because no quality is lost during editing, but too large to publish, so convert to MP3 afterwards.'

'Explain why GIF suits a club crest but not a team photo' – the crest has few colours so fits the 256-colour palette with no loss (1), compressed losslessly so edges stay sharp (1); the photo needs thousands of shades so a 256-colour palette causes banding/poor quality (1).

5.title: Software
terms: The core of the operating system, which loads programs into memory and unloads them, and allocates memory, secondary storage and processor time.
System software that manages a computer's hardware and software resources and acts as the interface between the hardware, the application software and the user.
An operating system that lets many users use one computer at the same time, sharing its resources by time-slicing while keeping each user's data private.
Sharing processor time by giving each user or task a short, fixed period of CPU time in turn, so all appear to run at once.
A state in which two or more threads or processes each wait for a resource held by another, so none of them can continue.
Dividing work between two or more processors or cores so that it is executed truly in parallel, mainly to increase speed.
Holding several programs in main memory at once and switching the single CPU between them, for example when one waits for I/O, although only one executes at any instant.
A memory management technique that divides memory into equal, fixed-size pages, which a page table maps to frames anywhere in physical memory.
A memory management technique that divides a program into variable-sized logical segments, such as modules or data structures, recorded in a segment table with base address and length.
A signal to the processor from hardware or software that an event needs attention; the current task is suspended while an interrupt service routine runs.
The program that is run to deal with a particular interrupt, after which the interrupted task is resumed.
A scheduling algorithm in which each process is given a fixed time slice of the processor in turn, unfinished processes returning to the back of the queue.
A program that allows the operating system to communicate with and control a specific hardware device by translating general requests into device-specific commands.
System software that performs one specific task to help manage, maintain or protect a computer, such as compression, backup, archiving or defragmentation.
A utility that rearranges the data on a magnetic hard disk so that each file occupies contiguous clusters and free space is grouped, reducing access time.
A translator that converts assembly language mnemonics into machine code, mostly one instruction for one instruction.
A translator that converts a whole high-level program into object code before it is executed, producing an executable file and reporting all errors together.
Processor-independent code, such as Java bytecode or C# CIL, produced by a compiler and run on each platform by a virtual machine or just-in-time compiler.
A translator that translates and executes a high-level program one statement at a time, without producing an executable file, stopping at the first error.
The first stage of compilation, in which comments and white space are removed, the source code is split into tokens and a symbol table of identifiers is built.
Programs designed to let the end user carry out specific tasks, such as word processing or booking tickets; they access the hardware through the operating system.
Application software that can be used for many different tasks without modification, such as a word processor or spreadsheet.
Application software designed to carry out one specific task or meet a particular business need.
Software written specifically to meet one organisation's requirements, by in-house developers or a third-party software house.
Ready-made software developed for a wide market and licensed to many customers, available immediately.
Software distributed with its source code under a licence that allows users to study, modify and redistribute it.
Software owned by an individual or company and distributed under a licence that keeps the source code secret and restricts copying and modification.
Electronic funds transfer at point of sale: payment by card at a till, where payment details are sent to the card issuer for authorisation and the funds are transferred electronically.
tips: 'State the purpose of an OS' is usually 2 marks: one for managing resources (name some: memory, processor, devices) and one for acting as an interface. Saying 'it runs the computer' earns nothing.
For 'describe a multi-user OS' the two points that examiners credit most are time-slicing (with what it achieves) and keeping each user's data private. Put both in your answer.

A 'two differences' question on paging and segmentation is marked as pairs: state the paging side and the contrasting segmentation side for each mark pair, e.g. 'pages are fixed size whereas segments are variable size'.
In a scenario question, tie each security function to a threat: 'access rights stop a receptionist opening patient records' earns more than a list of features.
When asked to explain the need for utilities, give the problem and how the utility solves it: 'files become fragmented over time, so a defragmenter is needed to restore access speed'.
Compiler/interpreter questions are marked in pairs: give the compiler side and the contrasting interpreter side for each difference.
Use the scenario: name the actual programs given and say what makes each generic or special purpose. Each correct definition plus a matching example usually earns 2 marks.
Each point needs a reason. 'Off-the-shelf is cheaper' scores less than 'off-the-shelf is cheaper because the development cost is shared among many customers'.

For 'explain two benefits of the web-based version', give the feature and its consequence in the scenario: 'updates are applied centrally on the server, so every member of staff always uses the latest version'.

To justify real-time, state the consequence of delay in the scenario: 'otherwise the same seat could be sold to two customers'. To justify batch, say the output is only needed periodically and the same processing applies to every record.

6.title: Web applications
terms: A global network of interconnected computer networks that use the TCP/IP protocols so that any connected device can communicate with any other.
A company that provides homes and businesses with a connection to the Internet, often with services such as email, domain registration and web hosting.
A service that stores a website's files on servers permanently connected to the Internet so the site can be accessed by users.
A computer, and the software running on it, that stores web pages and delivers them to browsers when requested using HTTP.
A service running over the Internet: a collection of linked web pages and resources, each with a unique address, accessed using HTTP and web browsers.
A distributed, hierarchical system of servers that translates domain names into IP addresses and shares updates when addresses change.
A unique numeric address assigned to a device on a network such as the Internet: 32 bits in IPv4 and 128 bits in IPv6.
The last label of a domain name, such as .uk, .ie or .com, which may indicate the country or type of organisation.
A standard protocol for transferring files of any type between computers, with user authentication, commonly used to upload website files to a web host.
Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure: HTTP sent over an encrypted TLS connection, with the server authenticated by a digital certificate.
Uniform resource locator: the full address of a resource on the Web, made up of the protocol, the domain name and the path or file name.
A small piece of text that a website asks the browser to store and that the browser returns with each later request, so the site can remember information about the user.
Data about a user's visit stored on the web server and identified by a session ID that the browser sends with each request.
Temporary storage of previously retrieved web content, in the browser or on a proxy server, checked before content is requested again from the web server.
Google's algorithm that ranks a page more highly the more pages link to it, giving more weight to links from highly ranked pages.
The search engine's store of information about every page visited by the crawler, such as its words, media and metadata, organised so that terms can be looked up quickly.
A program that automatically visits web pages, starting from seed pages and following every link, to collect information for a search engine's index.
An agreed specification, published by a recognised body, that lets products from different makers work together.
Code, usually JavaScript, that is downloaded with a web page and run by the user's browser.
A web page generated at the time it is requested, often from database data, so its content can change or be personalised.
Code that runs on the web server to process requests, access databases and generate pages before they are sent to the browser.
An attack in which SQL code is entered into an input field so that it is executed by the database, prevented by server-side validation and parameterised queries.
An application written for and installed on a specific operating system, with direct access to the device's hardware and the ability to work offline.
An application that runs in a web browser and is delivered from a server, processing user input and usually storing its data in a database on the server, without being installed on the device.
Government information and services provided electronically, usually online, to citizens, businesses and other organisations.
Services provided through electronic communication, usually the Internet, such as online shopping, banking, help desks and digital newspapers.
A website or page that provides consistent access to a number of connected services from a single starting point, often grouped into portlets.
A private network, usually of web pages and online services, within an organisation that only its authorised members can access.
Converting plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and a key so that only someone with the correct key can read it.
Encryption using a linked key pair: data encrypted with the freely available public key can only be decrypted with the owner's secret private key.
Encryption in which the same secret key is used both to encrypt and to decrypt the data.
An electronic document, issued and signed by a certificate authority, that links a public key to the verified identity of its owner.
A hash of a document encrypted with the sender's private key, used with the sender's public key to verify who sent the document and that it has not been altered.
Protocols that create an authenticated, encrypted link between two devices, such as a browser and a web server; TLS is the modern successor to SSL.
tips: Definition questions usually give one mark for what it is and one for what it does. 'A web server is a computer' scores half; add 'that stores web pages and sends them to browsers on request using HTTP'.
To identify sub-domains, peel labels off from the right one at a time and say which is a sub-domain of which.

'Which protocol and why' questions: FTP for uploading the pages to the server because it transfers files with authentication; HTTP(S) for a visitor viewing them because it is the protocol browsers use to request pages.
Statelessness questions often ask for both advantages (simple and efficient) and how a site still remembers a user (cookie or session ID sent with each request).
Learn the three components with what each does. A typical 6-mark question gives 2 marks per component: one for naming its job and one for a detail.
Link each body to concrete examples. 'The W3C sets standards for HTML and CSS so pages display consistently in all browsers' earns the marks; 'the W3C looks after the Web' does not.
A comparison answer should cover where the code runs, who can see it, effect on server load and response time, and why server-side checks are still needed.
Tie every point to the scenario and finish with a recommendation. 'Native, because the app must use the camera and work with no signal' beats a list of generic pros and cons.
For 'explain what is meant by a portal' give the definition and a concrete example, e.g. a council site linking bin collections, planning and rates in one place.
For 8-mark questions, examiners reward balance, application to the scenario and a reasoned judgement. Include at least one security measure and say what risk it reduces.
In 'evaluate' questions, say what each method protects and its limits: HTTPS protects data in transit but not a weak password or a phishing site with its own valid certificate.

7.title: Website development
terms: Hypertext Markup Language: the markup language that uses tags to define the structure and content of a web page, such as headings, paragraphs, lists, images and links.
The alt attribute of an image, giving a text description that is displayed if the image cannot load and is read aloud by screen readers.
The a tag, which creates a hyperlink; its href attribute gives the destination URL and the enclosed content is what the user clicks.
Extra information written inside an HTML opening tag as name="value" that refines the element, such as href, src or alt.
A code beginning with an ampersand and ending with a semicolon, such as < or ©, used to display a reserved or special character in HTML.
An HTML tag used as an opening and closing pair that encloses content, such as p … /p or a … /a.
An HTML tag that stands alone with no closing tag because it encloses no content, such as br, img or link.
Cascading Style Sheets: the language used to describe the presentation of web pages, such as colours, fonts, spacing and layout, separately from the content.
The part of a CSS rule that identifies which HTML elements the declarations apply to, e.g. an element name, a .class or an #id.
A separate .css file attached to web pages with the link tag so that one set of style rules controls the appearance of the whole site.
The way a nested (child) element takes on style properties such as colour and font from the element that contains it (its parent).
A style written in the style attribute of a single HTML element, affecting only that element and taking precedence over style sheet rules.
The rule that when the same property is defined in more than one place, the definition closest to the element, such as an inline style, takes priority.
A diagram, usually a tree, showing all the pages of a website and how they are linked.
An annotated sketch of the layout of each web page, showing the position of navigation, headings, text, images and other elements.
The group of people a website is designed for, described by factors such as age, interests, abilities, accessibility needs and the devices they use.
A navigation structure in which the home page links to main sections, which in turn link to their own sub-pages.
A navigation structure in which pages are visited in a fixed sequence using next and previous links.
Web design in which the layout adapts automatically to the size of the screen being used, for example through flexible layouts and CSS media queries.

Web Content Accessibility Guidelines: the W3C's international standard for accessible web content, with success criteria at levels A, AA and AAA under the principles perceivable, operable, understandable and robust.
Processing carried out by the browser on the user's device, such as validating form input or changing the page, without contacting the server.
Processing carried out on the web server after a request is submitted, such as querying and updating a database and generating the response page.
A hyperlink whose destination does not exist, producing an error such as 404 Not Found.
tips: If asked what goes in the head and what goes in the body: head = information about the page (title, character set, style sheet link); body = the content the user sees.
Changing a bulleted list into a numbered list only needs the outer ul tags changed to ol; the li items stay the same.

'Describe container and empty tags' needs a definition and an example of each: 'p is a container tag because it has an opening and a closing tag around the paragraph text; br is empty because it encloses nothing'.
In 'how will this text appear' questions, deal with each property separately and use the words inherited and overridden/precedence with a reason for each.

'Explain the benefits of linked (external) style sheets' wants explanation, not a list: say what changes (one edit) and why it matters (every linked page updates, keeping a consistent house style and reducing maintenance).

'What does a site map show and why is it produced?' needs both parts: it shows all the pages and how they link (1), so that the structure and navigation are planned and no page is missed or unreachable (1).
For a navigation question, choose and justify using the context: name the structure, describe how it would be organised for this site, and give the reason it suits the users or task.
Name a specific feature, say who it helps and how: 'alt text describes each image so a screen reader can read it aloud to a blind user' earns marks; 'make it accessible for blind people' does not.
Apply both terms to the scenario. 'One happens on the computer and the other on the server' earns little; say what the browser checks and what the server retrieves, updates and returns.
When asked why data is validated again on the server, give both halves: client checks can be bypassed (say how), and the server protects the data/database (say from what).
Test plan answers need specific tests with the data and expected outcome, not 'check it works'. Two good tests with outcomes usually earn 4 marks.

1.title: Network resources
terms: A network covering a single site or building, with infrastructure owned and managed by the organisation.
A network covering a town or city, linking sites such as council buildings or university campuses.
A network covering a large geographical area, connecting LANs using telecommunications links leased from third parties; the internet is the largest WAN.
The area within which wireless devices can connect to a network through a wireless access point.
A logical numerical address that identifies a device on a network so that data can be routed to it.
A unique 48-bit hardware address assigned to a network interface card, used to deliver frames on a local network.
A device that connects networks using dissimilar media by converting the signal from one to the other, for example between fibre optic and copper cable.
Hardware that connects a device to a network medium, converting data into signals, and holds the device's unique MAC address.
A device that regenerates and amplifies a signal that has weakened or distorted over a long distance so the data can travel further.
A computer on a network that manages and shares resources, such as files, printers, web pages or email, and responds to requests from other nodes.
The central connection point of a network that reads the destination address of each packet and forwards it only to the node it is addressed to (also called a switch).
A device that allows wireless devices to connect to a wired LAN using Wi-Fi.
An IP address lent to a device each time it connects, from a pool shared by the network (usually by a DHCP server), so it may change.
An IP address that is permanently assigned to a device, usually by hand, so other devices can always find it at the same address.
A network with no dedicated server in which all computers have equal status and each both supplies resources to and uses resources from the others.
A network in which one or more dedicated servers control storage, backup, software, printing and security for client computers, whose users log on to use the resources.
The main cable of a bus network to which every node is attached, with a terminator at each end.
A special message passed from node to node in a ring network; only the node holding it may transmit.
The physical or logical arrangement of the devices (nodes) and links in a network, such as bus, star, ring or mesh.
tips: Table questions often ask for a scope and a communication medium for each network and say you may not repeat an answer. Plan it first: LAN – single building, Ethernet cable; MAN – city, fibre optic; WAN – global, communication satellites.

'Distinguish' questions need a matched pair: say what the IP address identifies and what the MAC address identifies, e.g. 'the MAC address identifies the physical NIC on the LAN, whereas the IP address identifies the device's connection on the internet'.
For 'features of a P2P network' four quick marks are: no dedicated server; equal status; each supplies resources; each consumes resources. Do not drift into advantages unless asked.

Evaluate questions with 'Quality of written communication' are banded. Top-band answers describe both topologies accurately, apply the criterion to each, and finish with a justified judgement. Keep to the criterion asked – a security question gains nothing from cost.

2.title: Protocols, transmission media and errors
terms: The International Telecommunication Union, a United Nations agency that manages use of the radio-frequency spectrum, sets worldwide telecommunication standards and helps countries develop their networks.
A set of rules that governs how data is formatted, transmitted and received so that devices can communicate.
The World Wide Web Consortium, an international body that develops open protocols and guidelines for the web so that it works for everyone and keeps growing.
The top three layers of the OSI model – application, presentation and session – which provide the interface and services for users' programs.
A seven-layer reference model of network communication: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation and application.
The bottom four layers of the OSI model – transport, network, data link and physical – which manage network traffic and the accurate delivery of data.
Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection: devices listen before sending, detect collisions, and wait a random, increasing time before retrying.
An electronic document, issued and signed by a certificate authority, that binds a public key to the identity of its owner.
Converting plaintext into unreadable ciphertext using an algorithm and a key, so only holders of the correct key can read it.
The standard protocol for wired LANs (IEEE 802.3), defining the cables and connectors as well as how data is framed and sent.
HTTP sent over an encrypted TLS connection, so web data cannot be read or altered in transit and the server's identity is verified.
A method of transmission in which data is split into addressed packets that travel independently across shared links, possibly by different routes, and are reassembled at the destination.
The family of protocols used on the internet: TCP splits data into numbered packets and reassembles them in order, and IP addresses each packet and forwards it across networks.
An access method in which a token is passed from device to device and only the device holding it may transmit, so collisions cannot occur.
A short-range, low-power radio protocol that lets devices pair and exchange data directly, peer-to-peer, in a small network called a piconet.
A small ad hoc network formed when Bluetooth devices pair with each other.
The IEEE 802.11 protocol for wireless LANs, in which devices with wireless adapters connect by radio to a network through a wireless access point.
Radio-frequency identification: a reader's radio waves activate a tag, which sends back the data stored on its chip, with no line of sight needed.
Voice over Internet Protocol: making telephone calls over IP networks such as the internet by converting speech into digital data packets.
The capacity of a communication channel (the range of frequencies it can carry), which determines the maximum rate at which data can be transmitted.
A high-capacity transmission method that carries multiple signals on different frequencies at the same time over one medium.
Digital subscriber line: broadband over a copper telephone line that sends data at frequencies above those used for voice, so calls and data share the line.
Metal cable with a central copper conductor surrounded by insulation and a braided copper shield that protects against interference.
A transmission medium that carries data as pulses of light along glass fibres, giving very high bandwidth over long distances with immunity to electrical interference.
Copper cable made of pairs of insulated wires twisted together to reduce interference; unshielded (UTP) or shielded (STP).
Error checking with a parity bit for every byte (row) and a parity byte for every column, so a single flipped bit can be located where the failing row and column cross and then corrected.
A parity scheme in which the parity bit is set so that each byte contains an even number of 1s.
A parity scheme in which the parity bit is set so that each byte contains an odd number of 1s.
An extra bit added to a group of bits so that the total number of 1s is even (even parity) or odd (odd parity), used to detect transmission errors.
A value calculated from a block of data and sent with it; the receiver recalculates it and compares to detect errors.
An error-detection method in which the data is divided by an agreed binary generator and the remainder is sent and checked by the receiver; effective against burst errors.
Error detection in which the receiver sends a copy of the received data back to the sender, which compares it with the original and re-transmits if they differ.
tips: A one-mark definition must contain both ideas: rules and different devices communicating. 'A protocol is a set of rules' alone is not enough.
Layer descriptions are worth 3–4 marks each. Give the layer's function, a concrete detail (e.g. 'converts bits into light pulses in fibre'), and which layers it exchanges data with.
For CSMA/CD, describe the sequence: listen → send if free → collision detected → random wait → retry with longer waits. Four steps, four marks.
In a 'compare' question give similarities too: both are wireless radio protocols with fairly short range. Then the differences: network versus device-to-device, range, speed, power, security.

RFID versus barcode comparisons are banded (QWC). Explain how each works first, then compare on matched criteria – line of sight, speed, data, durability, cost – and finish with a judgement for the context.
Each term is usually worth 2 marks. For bandwidth give capacity plus how it is measured (Hz or bps with an example). For broadband give many signals at once plus always-on high-speed access.

'Name a medium and describe how data is transferred' wants the mechanism: for fibre, 'modulated pulses of light along fine glass strands, one direction per strand, with separate strands for each direction'.
These are 6-mark banded questions. Describe both media, evaluate both against the named criterion only, and end with a clear judgement. A table of facts without evaluation stays in the lower band.

In 'evaluate parity' questions use the given bytes: show the count of 1s before and after, state whether the parity changed, and say whether the error is detected. Then generalise: odd numbers of errors caught, even numbers missed, location unknown.

For 'describe how CRC detects and corrects errors' (6 marks): value appended before sending → block divided by a fixed number → remainder is the check value → recalculated after transmission → mismatch means an error → data corrected or re-transmitted.

3.title: Databases
terms: A situation in which copies of the same data item hold different values, so it is unclear which is correct; usually caused by redundant data being updated in some places but not others.
The unnecessary storage of the same data item more than once.
Software that sits between users or programs and the stored data, allowing a database to be defined, queried and updated while controlling security, integrity, concurrent access, backup and recovery.
An object, person, place or event about which data is stored; it becomes a table in a relational database.
A database held as a single table or file of records with no relationships to any other table.
An attribute in one table that is the primary key of another table, used to create a relationship between the two tables.
An attribute, or combination of attributes, chosen to uniquely identify each record in a table; its value must be unique and never null.
A database in which data is stored in separate tables (relations), each about one entity, linked by primary and foreign keys.
A link between two entities showing how their occurrences are associated, implemented by a foreign key.
A design-stage model of the data, independent of any DBMS, identifying the entities, their attributes and keys, and the relationships between them.
An implementation model derived from the logical model for a specific DBMS, specifying every table, column, data type, key and constraint.
A property or characteristic of an entity; it becomes a field in a table.
Any attribute, or minimal set of attributes, that could uniquely identify every record and so could be chosen as the primary key.
A primary key made up of two or more attributes which together, but not separately, uniquely identify a record.
A non-unique field that is indexed to allow fast searching or sorting, such as Surname.
A referential integrity option in which deleting a parent record automatically deletes all its related child records.
Storing the same data item more than once in a database, in one table or in separate tables; also called data redundancy.
How many occurrences of one entity can be linked to one occurrence of another: 1:1 (one-to-one), 1:M (one-to-many) or M:N (many-to-many).
A child record whose foreign key refers to a parent record that does not exist.
The rule that every foreign key value must match an existing primary key value in the related table (or be null where allowed), preventing orphan records.
A diagram showing the entities in a system as boxes and the relationships between them as lines, with crow's feet marking the 'many' ends.
An entity introduced to resolve a many-to-many relationship into two one-to-many relationships; its key is usually a composite of the two foreign keys.
Describes a field holding a single, indivisible value rather than a list or group of values.
A relation with no repeating groups in which every attribute holds a single atomic value and every record is identified by a primary key.
A relationship A → B in which each value of attribute A determines exactly one value of attribute B.
A formal process of organising attributes into relations to minimise data redundancy and prevent update, insertion and deletion anomalies.
Where a non-key attribute depends on only part of a composite primary key.
A set of attributes that occurs several times for a single value of the key in un-normalised data.
A relation in 1NF with no partial dependencies, so every non-key attribute depends on the whole of a composite key.
A relation in 2NF with no transitive dependencies, so every non-key attribute depends on the key, the whole key and nothing but the key.
Where a non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute rather than directly on the primary key.
The unintended loss of data about one thing when a record about something else is deleted.
The inability to add data about one thing because data about something else, needed to complete the record or its key, does not yet exist.
An inconsistency caused when a fact stored in several rows is changed in some but not all of them.
A central store of metadata describing every table, field, data type, key, validation rule, index, relationship and access right in a database.
The accuracy, completeness, consistency and validity of data throughout its life.
A value that the DBMS places in a field automatically when a new record is created, unless the user enters a different value.
A sorted data structure of field values and pointers to records that lets the DBMS locate, sort and join records quickly without scanning the whole table.
A field whose value must be chosen from a fixed list or from the records of another table, rather than typed freely.
Data that describes other data, such as a field's name, data type, size and validation rule.
An automatic check that data entered is reasonable and obeys defined rules, such as a presence, range, type, format or lookup check.
A rule defined on a table, such as PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, NOT NULL, UNIQUE or CHECK, that the DBMS enforces on every change to the data.
The part of SQL used to create and change the structure of a database, e.g. CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE.
The part of SQL used to retrieve and change the data held in tables, e.g. SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE.
The rule that every table has a primary key whose values are unique and never null.
Structured Query Language: the standard declarative language for defining, querying and manipulating relational databases.
An SQL function that calculates a single value from a set of rows, such as COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN or MAX.
An SQL clause that groups rows sharing a value so that aggregate functions are calculated for each group, giving one result row per group.
An operation that combines rows from two or more tables by matching a foreign key with the related primary key.
A symbol used with LIKE to match unknown characters: % matches any sequence of characters and _ matches exactly one character.
A visual way of querying a database in which the user selects tables and fields and enters criteria into a grid or form, and the DBMS generates the SQL automatically.
tips: 'Describe the main features of a relational database' (4 marks) – four separate features: tables of records; unique primary key; tables linked by primary/foreign keys; one query across many tables / minimal redundancy. Do not spend the answer on what a flat file is.

Each model is usually worth 2–3 marks. Say when it is produced, whether it depends on the DBMS, and what it contains – entities/relationships/attributes/keys for logical; tables/columns/data types/keys for physical.
Define and exemplify from the given table: 'a composite key is made of more than one attribute that together identify a record (1), e.g. OrderID with ProdID in the order-line table (1)'.

Data duplication and inconsistency questions almost always say 'by referring to the table'. One mark for the definition, one for a real example from the table – a repeated name, or one ID with two different values.
Marks are given per entity and per relationship with the crow's foot at the correct end. Draw neat boxes, label each with a singular noun, and check the final logical design has no M:N lines left.
'Explain why the table is not in 1NF/2NF/3NF' (2 marks): name the problem (repeating group / partial dependency / non-key dependency) and quote the attributes involved from the given table.

'Describe two advantages' (4 marks) needs two different advantages, each with its consequence: 'less duplicated data (1), so less storage is needed (1)'; 'fewer conflicting copies (1), so the data can be trusted more (1)'.

Marks are given stage by stage, roughly one per correct table. Write each table in the form NAME(Key, Attribute, ForeignKey*), and if a stage changes nothing (e.g. 2NF is already 3NF) say so – that statement earns a mark.
'State three items of metadata' – give three distinct items (field name, data type, validation rule), not three examples of one item.

Use the exact table and field names in the question, choose sensible sizes (a postcode needs 8 characters, not 255), and include PRIMARY KEY and FOREIGN KEY … REFERENCES whenever keys are mentioned – they are usually separate marks.

Retrieval questions are marked per clause: SELECT with the right fields (1), FROM the right table (1), WHERE with the right condition (1), ORDER BY with DESC if asked (1). Use the exact field names from the question.
Marks are usually per clause: UPDATE + table (1), SET (1), WHERE (1). Leaving out the WHERE when one is needed loses the mark and changes the meaning entirely.

Evaluate questions are banded with quality of written communication. Describe QBE and SQL, then evaluate both for the task named – 'creating a database' and 'generating queries' are different tasks – and give a reasoned conclusion.

4.title: AI, expert systems and robotics
terms: The ability of computer systems to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence, such as recognising images and speech, understanding language and making decisions.
A branch of AI in which algorithms improve their performance at a task by learning patterns from data rather than following explicitly programmed rules.
A test proposed by Alan Turing in which a player questions a hidden human and a hidden machine by text; if the player cannot reliably tell which is the machine, it is judged intelligent.
The way a neural network learns: the difference between its actual and intended output is passed back through the layers and used to adjust the connection weights.
A neural network in which signals pass in one direction, from the input units through the hidden layers to the output units.
A machine learning model made of layers of connected nodes whose weighted connections are adjusted during training; many layers form a deep learning model.
A computer system that emulates the decision-making of a human expert in a narrow domain using a knowledge base of rules and an inference engine.
The part of an expert system's interface that shows the user which rules and facts were used to reach a conclusion.
The part of an expert system that applies the rules in the knowledge base to the facts supplied, by forward or backward chaining, to reach conclusions.
The part of an expert system that stores the facts and IF–THEN rules gathered from human experts.
The narrow field of knowledge that an expert system covers, such as diagnosing engine faults.
A specialist who gathers knowledge from human experts and encodes it as facts and rules in an expert system's knowledge base.
An expert system with an empty knowledge base: the development environment, inference engine and interface into which the rules and facts for a particular application are entered.
Reasoning with degrees of truth between 0 and 1 rather than true or false, so that decisions can be made from vague, uncertain or incomplete data.
Rules of thumb derived from an expert's experience and intuition rather than from logic alone, allowing judgement when facts are uncertain.
The reduction in the skill needed for a job because technology now performs the skilled part of the work.
A device that samples an analogue signal, such as sound from a microphone, and converts it into digital (binary) data.
The branch of AI concerned with computers analysing, understanding and generating human language in its natural spoken or written form.
Hardware and software that input and digitise spoken words and decode them into text or commands for the computer.
A device that carries out a physical action, such as moving a motor or opening a valve, in response to a control signal.
The tool fitted to the end of a robot arm that carries out the task, such as a gripper, suction cup, welding torch or paint spray.
The design and use of programmable machines that sense their environment, process the data and carry out physical actions.
A device that measures a physical quantity, such as temperature, movement or light, and converts it into data a computer can process.
A hand-held control unit used to program a robot by specifying, step by step, the movements it must make.
Using technology to carry out tasks with little or no human involvement.
Pain or damage to muscles, tendons or nerves caused by repeated movements such as typing or using a mouse.
tips: A 2–3 mark definition needs three ideas: intelligence/human abilities, modelled by computer systems, and so machines can learn/adapt or react like humans.

'How is the test carried out?' – name the three participants and their roles, say the player does not know which is which, and say what counts as a pass. 'State its purpose' – to decide whether a machine's behaviour is indistinguishable from a human's.

A 6-mark 'main features' answer: units in layers (input/hidden/output) – connections between layers – weights – weighted sum and threshold – feedforward flow – learning by backpropagation. Six features, six marks.

'State the two other components' – if the question names one (often the knowledge base), give the other two: inference engine and user interface. Do not give 'expert' or 'knowledge engineer' – they are people, not components.
For the inference engine, use the verbs examiners look for: interrogates the knowledge base, poses questions to the user, applies the rules, draws inferences/conclusions.
These terms are usually asked three at a time for 9 marks (3 each). For each give: what it is, what it contains or does, and how it is used in this expert system – use the scenario in the question.

A top-band evaluation describes how the system works in the context given, gives benefits and drawbacks for that context, and ends with a justified judgement. Generic lists of advantages stay in the lower band.
NLP versus voice recognition: voice recognition converts sound into words or commands; NLP works out the meaning of language, spoken or written. A system can do either without the other.
'Describe two uses of NLP' (4 marks): name the use and explain what NLP does in it, e.g. 'spam filtering (1) – the text of each email is analysed to identify unwanted messages and block them (1)'.

'Explain the term robotics' (4 marks): a combination of disciplines (1) – name them: computer science, mechanical and electrical engineering (1) – to design, build and operate robots (1) – using sensors and feedback (1).
For 'describe two benefits of robots in this case' the second mark needs the reason: 'improved quality (1) because the robot repeats the same movements exactly every time (1)'.

5.title: Mobile technology, data mining and the cloud
terms: Equipment that controls one or more base stations, sets up calls and manages handoffs between cells, working with the mobile switching centre.
The area, drawn as a hexagon, served by one base station and its masts in a mobile phone network.
The automatic transfer of a mobile call to a new base station as the user moves into another cell, so the call is not interrupted.
The exchange of a mobile network that sets up and routes calls and texts, tracks where phones are and connects the network to the PSTN.
The public switched telephone network: the worldwide landline telephone system of telephones wired to public exchanges.

Data sets so large, fast-arriving or varied that they cannot be stored or processed efficiently with traditional database tools; characterised by volume, velocity and variety (often also veracity and value).
The process of analysing large data sets with statistical and machine-learning techniques to discover previously unknown patterns, relationships and trends.
A large central store of integrated, historical, read-only data copied from many operational systems and organised for analysis and decision-making.
A data mining technique that identifies unusual records which may need investigation or may be errors, such as a suspicious card payment.
Any information relating to an identified or identifiable living individual.
The on-demand delivery of computing resources such as servers, storage and software over the internet, usually paid for by subscription or use.
A deployment that links a private cloud or on-premises systems with public cloud services so data and applications can move between them.
A cloud model in which the provider supplies virtualised servers, storage and networking, and the customer manages the operating system and software.
A cloud model in which the provider supplies and manages the hardware, operating system and runtime so customers only develop and manage their own applications.
Cloud infrastructure dedicated to a single organisation, located on its premises or hosted on dedicated hardware.
Cloud infrastructure owned by a provider and shared by many organisations over the internet.
A central computer centre containing a large number of linked servers, used by cloud providers to host the services they supply.
A cloud model in which complete application software is hosted and maintained by the provider and accessed by users over the internet, usually by subscription.
Grouping servers so that they act as a single system, sharing work through load balancing and parallel processing to meet demand.
A block of a cloud server's resources allocated to one client as its own virtual server, with processing and storage that can be adjusted dynamically as demand changes.
Hardware and software reserved for the sole use of one client, who pays for all of it whether it is used or not.
Software that creates, runs and manages virtual machines on a physical host, sharing its resources between them.
A software emulation of a complete computer, with its own operating system, running on shared physical hardware.
The use of software to create virtual versions of hardware resources, allowing several virtual machines to run on one physical computer.
A backup that copies all files changed since the last full backup.
A backup that copies only the files changed since the last backup of any type.
The person or organisation that decides the purposes for which, and the means by which, personal data is processed, and is responsible for compliance.
A risk to an organisation's systems or data from employees or contractors who misuse their legitimate access, deliberately or accidentally.
tips: In the 6-mark 'make a call while travelling' question, use every term you are given in the right order – cell and mast, base station controller, mobile switching centre, handoffs as the caller moves, PSTN for the landline. Explaining each term separately is not required; the route of the call is.

'What is meant by data mining?' (4 marks): analysing/sorting (1) large data sets/big data (1) to identify patterns and relationships (1) to predict future trends (1). Add 'automatic', 'data warehouse' or 'several sources' for extra points.
For 'how digital technology is used to gather, store, process and analyse' give at least one specific technology for each of the four verbs.
'Describe two ways a sector uses big data' (4 marks): each way needs what (e.g. optimise prices) and how (by analysing spending habits and competitors' prices).

A 4-mark 'how could data mining threaten privacy' answer: what data is stored (1), who could use it (1), for unauthorised purposes (1) that the person has not agreed to or does not know about (1) – applied to the people in the question.
A 4-mark definition: internet/server farms (1), large computing companies/third party (1), providing services (1) normally provided by a LAN (1).
Each term is usually 2 marks: one for what it is, one for a detail – 'a hosted instance is one client's virtual server (1) whose share of processing and storage grows and shrinks with demand (1)'.
'Describe how the cloud provides data storage' (4 marks): data saved off-site (1) on a remote database (1) provided by a third party (1) and reached over the internet instead of local storage (1).

6.title: Legislation and ethics
terms: The data protection principle that personal data must be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the purpose.
A person or organisation that processes personal data on behalf of, and on the instructions of, a data controller.
The identified or identifiable living individual whom personal data is about.

The independent UK regulator for data protection and information rights, including freedom of information, which replaced the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) on 30 September 2026; it issues guidance, investigates and enforces.
A request by an individual for a copy of the personal data an organisation holds about them; normally free and answered within one month.
The automatic legal right of the creator of an original work, including software, to control its copying, adaptation and distribution; protected by the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988.
Creations of the mind, such as software, music, designs and writing, that the law protects as the property of their creator.
Software whose source code is published under a licence that allows anyone to use, study, modify and redistribute it, subject to the licence's conditions.
A legal agreement setting out how a piece of software may be used, installed, copied and distributed.
The illegal copying, modifying, distributing or downloading of software without the owner's permission or a valid licence.

UK law creating offences of unauthorised access to computer material, access with intent to commit further offences, unauthorised acts that impair a computer, acts causing serious damage, and making or supplying tools for these offences.
Malicious software, such as viruses, worms, trojans, spyware and ransomware, designed to damage, disrupt, steal from or gain unauthorised control of a computer system.
Accessing a computer system or data without permission or beyond the access one is entitled to – an offence under section 1 of the Computer Misuse Act 1990.
An organisation's written rules on how employees may use its computers, networks and data, including the disciplinary consequences of misuse.
Authentication that requires evidence from two or more different categories – something you know, have or are.
Systematic unfairness in the outputs of an algorithm or AI system, usually caused by biased or unrepresentative training data or design choices.
The discouragement of lawful behaviour, such as free expression, because people know or fear they are being monitored.
The monitoring of people's behaviour, activities or communications, for example by CCTV, facial recognition, location tracking or interception.
tips: 'Identify four other principles' – give four different principles, worded as rules about personal data. Do not repeat the one in the question, and do not invent time limits.
For licensing questions, name the Act, say exactly what has been copied or shared without permission, and state a consequence – legal action, damages, fines or reputational harm.
In scenario questions, identify each act separately and name the section that fits: viewing, then altering, then distributing are three different offences.

'Describe three steps an organisation should take so employees comply with the Computer Misuse Act' – each step needs the action and its effect: 'an acceptable use policy (1) so every employee knows what they may access and the disciplinary consequences (1)'.

Ethics questions want questions and tensions, not law. For 2 marks per issue, raise the consideration and explain why it matters to the people affected, e.g. 'the decision may be based on biased data (1), so some applicants are refused unfairly (1)'.

The 9-mark 'discuss the ethical considerations of companies using personal information' question is banded with QWC. Organise it as capture → storage → analysis → sharing, give a benefit and a concern at each stage, and finish with a reasoned judgement.
